author: AWSM
title: Against the Ritual: Why Anarchists in Aotearoa Refuse the Ballot Box
content:
Aotearoa Workers Solidarity Movement

It’s a strange thing to be told, over and over again, that you’re the unreasonable one for refusing to participate in something that, historically and globally, anarchists have treated with deep suspicion at best and outright hostility at worst. In Aotearoa New Zealand, saying anarchists should abstain from elections is still treated as fringe, sectarian, even irresponsible. You’ll be told you’re letting the Right win, that you’re abandoning vulnerable people, that you’re indulging in ideological purity while others suffer. Yet if you zoom out, even slightly, this position is neither new nor particularly extreme. It is, in fact, one of the oldest and most consistent threads in anarchist thought.

So why does it feel so controversial here? Part of it is that New Zealand has cultivated a very particular political culture, one that leans heavily on the myth of fairness, moderation, and incremental progress. Electoral politics here is framed less as a site of domination and more as a kind of collective moral project. Voting is not just a tactic, it is a ritual of belonging. To abstain is not simply to opt out of a strategy, but to step outside what is imagined as the shared ethical life of the nation.

Anarchism, at its core, has never been about belonging to the nation. It has always been about refusing the structures that demand obedience in the first place. Historically, anarchists have been remarkably consistent on this point. From the late nineteenth century through to the present, anarchist movements across Europe, the Americas, and beyond have argued that participation in parliamentary systems does not challenge power but legitimises it. The state, from this perspective, is not a neutral tool that can be wielded for good or ill depending on who holds office. It is a structure built to organise domination, class domination above all, and elections function as a way of renewing consent to that structure.

This isn’t an abstract argument. It emerges from lived experience. Again and again, movements that have placed their hopes in electoral change have found those hopes blunted, redirected, or outright betrayed. Radical parties moderate once they enter parliament. Transformative demands get watered down into policy tweaks. The machinery of the state absorbs opposition and spits it back out as something far less threatening.

Anarchists noticed this early. That’s why abstentionism, refusing to participate in elections, became a defining feature of many anarchist traditions. It isn’t about apathy. It is about clarity. If you believe that the state is fundamentally structured to maintain hierarchy and exploitation, then participating in its rituals starts to look less like pragmatism and more like complicity.

Globally, this position has never really gone away. It has shifted, adapted, been debated internally, but it remains widely understood. In some contexts, anarchists engage tactically with elections, supporting specific reforms, for instance, but often while maintaining a critical distance. In others, abstention remains the default. Which brings us back to Aotearoa. Here, abstention feels different. Not because the arguments against electoralism are weaker, but because the social and political context reshapes how those arguments are heard. New Zealand’s relative stability, its small size, and its carefully managed image as a progressive democracy all contribute to a sense that the system more or less works. Not perfectly, of course, but well enough that participation feels meaningful.

This is where the controversy really sits. When anarchists in New Zealand call for abstention, they are not just critiquing the state in the abstract. They are challenging a widely held belief that the system is capable of delivering justice if only the right people are elected, and that belief runs deep. You can see it in the way political debate is framed. Elections are treated as moments of possibility, of hope, of collective agency. Campaigns are saturated with language about change, about making a difference, about shaping the future. Even when people are disillusioned, the solution offered is usually more engagement, vote harder, get the right party in.

Against this backdrop, abstention looks like withdrawal. It can be read as giving up, as refusing to fight on the terrain where outcomes are decided. And in a context where harm is real and immediate, where people are struggling with …

author: The Dhadjowa Foundation
title: Daily Reporting: Jeffrey Winmar inquest, Day 7, April 9th, 2026
content:
The coronal inquest into the death of 28-year-old Noongar man Jeffrey Winmar resumed for its seventh day of session this morning.

Today we heard medical evidence from the doctors involved in Jeffrey’s care and two expert medical panels.

Prior to calling the first Witness, Mr Nathwani, Counsel acting on behalf of Jeffrey’s family addresses the Coroner, “some of the family may not be present today due to the nature of the evidence.”

Today’s summary includes details from the autopsy findings after Jeffrey’s passing. This information is distressing and we encourage people to take care while reading this summary.

The first witness called to give evidence is Dr Sayed Hassen. Dr Hassen is a surgeon, specialising in issues concerning the liver. He performed two surgeries on Jeffrey after he was taken to Box Hill Hospital via ambulance on 9 November.

While Dr Hassen did not have direct contact with Jeffrey following his immediate presentation to Box Hill Hospital, according to Dr Hasseen, Jeffrey was “critically unwell with a poor prognosis” upon his arrival at Box Hill Hospital.

Dr Hasseen is questioned about the handover Box Hill Hospital received from Ambulance Victoria and Victoria Police.

Ms Wong: It appears that the treating team had not been told that Jeffrey had jumped from a height of 3 meters?

Dr Hasseen: No, I don’t recall reading that initially, but we did know there was a pursuit of some kind.

When asked if this information would have earlier drawn the hospital’s attention to the possibility of internal injuries, Dr Haseen gives evidence that he does not believe that it would have materially changed Jeffrey’s treatment plan.

We learn that Jeffrey was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit at around 9:00pm, at which point Jeffrey was intubated and not breathing on his own. When asked about his condition at this point in time, Dr Hasseen expresses: “[Jeffrey] was more unwell than most patients in intensive care..his state was critical in more ways than one. “

After Jeffrey was transferred to the ICU a fast scan was done by an ICU consultant who noted free fluid around Jeffrey’s internal organs, which they believed to be blood.

We learn that two to three litres of blood were found in Jeffrey’s abdomen during the first surgery conducted by Dr Hassen.

Counsel Assisting puts it to Dr Hasseen that one of the concerns of Jeffrey’s family is that he was in hospital for a period of hours and that the internal bleeding that Jeffery experienced was missed by medical staff.

When asked to respond to this concern, Dr Hasseen states there were many things contributing to Jeffrey’s medical condition at this point in time, including multiple cardiac arrests.

When asked if the injury that Jeffrey sustained to his liver likely contributed to the cardiac arrest that Jeffrey experienced, Dr Hasseen gives evidence that it is unlikely, going on to express “he wasn’t behaving like someone who had a significant internal bleed at that time”.

Dr Hasseen goes on to give evidence that the pattern of injuries –  including the injuries to his livers and ribs – were compatible with injuries that may have been sustained from CPR.

It is later put to Dr Hasseen by Mr Nathwani, Counsel acting on behalf of Jeffrey’s father, that Jeffrey complained of sore ribs in the initial moments after he first lost consciousness under the tree.

Mr Nathwani: Would it be relevant for medical practitioners to have known that he complained of sore ribs before CPR?

Dr Hasseen: Yes it would be, it suggests something else happened at this point.

Mr Nathwani: Indicative of an issue isn’t it?

Mr Nathwani: Would it be relevant for medical practitioners to have known that Jeffrey complained of sore ribs before CPR?

Dr Hasseen: Yes it would be, it suggests something else happened at this point.

Mr Nathwani: Were you aware that either you or one of your colleagues specifically asked the family whether Jeffrey had been in a fight?

Ms Wong: Jeffrey’s mother Ursulla, has a distinct recollection that you spoke to her after the first laparotomy, and that you asked her whether Jeffrey had been in a fight. Is it your evidence that you don’t remember saying that?

Dr Hasseen: It was about two and a half years ago. Look, it’s possible that I have spoken to her, but I can’t recall whether there was something that prompted me to ask the question. The pattern of bruising might have prompted me to ask a question as to why there was bruising… I don’t recall that …

author: Ahmed Ashmawy
title: Alexandria’s Amreya shuts factory to striking workers
content:
Workers sought intervention from authorities on Sunday after management at Misr al-Amreya Spinning and Weaving Company in Alexandria decided to suspend operations at the factory indefinitely, according to four workers who spoke to Mada Masr.

The management’s statement said the shutdown was to allow for routine maintenance, inventory and reviews. But the workers said they view the move as punishment for their ongoing strike against under-payment.

Hundreds of workers at the company, which is owned by Banque Misr, began a strike in late July, to protest the miscalculation of a “special allowance” bonus to which they are entitled.

The workers told Mada Masr at the time that the company is calculating their bonuses as a percentage of their baseline wages, rather than as a percentage of their insured wages — effectively reducing the bonus value.

The base wage is around a third of the value of the insured wage, as per a worker’s payslip that Mada Masr reviewed last month.

A new social insurance law ratified in July obliges public sector companies to pay a “special allowance” bonus and to calculate it at the rate of 12 percent of the insured wage. Worker representatives speaking to Mada Masr last week said that the company owner has said Amreya is a private company exempt from the requirement, but the head of the company’s workers union committee, Mohamed al-Sawy, told Mada Masr that the company committed to an agreement five years ago that it would keep worker privileges at Amreya consistent with those in the public sector.

Throughout the strike, management and the company’s union committee tried to persuade workers to return to their jobs while their demands were being considered. The workers refused, and some received implicit threats, their representatives told Mada Masr. One quoted his manager as telling him, “What’s coming is not going to be good.”

Management issued a notice on Thursday saying it was “continuously examining and studying the legitimate rights of workers” in order to present their findings to the relevant authorities. The notice added that these rights “are safeguarded through unity.”

The striking workers rejected what came in the notice, as it did not specify any clear action or timeline for implementing their demands, according to the workers.

Management shuts company premises to workers

It was the following day that the Alexandria company’s management issued a notice suspending work, restricting attendance to “workers who are called in to manage the extensive inventorying operations,” while “salaries and wages stipulated by law will continue to be paid on their scheduled dates.”

Copy of Misr al-Amreya Spinning and Weaving Company management’s Friday notice.

On Saturday morning, employees tried to reach work by public transportation after the company withheld the buses that normally transport them to work from different areas, according to the workers. But police, deployed heavily at the railway crossing leading to the gate, blocked them from reaching the factory.

Fearing wage deductions over the closure, some workers went to the police station to file incident reports and lodged complaints with the labor office over their demands and the closure decision. Others filed similar complaints on Sunday.

The four company workers who spoke to Mada Masr said they were among those filing complaints with their local labor directorate on Sunday over management’s indefinite suspension of operations at the factory.

Amreya previously closed its factory for a month in 2015 after workers went on strike to demand the payment of incentives and bonuses in line with those granted at other companies in the spinning and weaving sector.

Workers at Amreya also staged a strike in February over wage reductions, which took the form of higher taxes and increased social insurance deductions. In April, they went on strike again, demanding higher wages, an increase in production bonuses and higher hazard pay.

author: A.N.A.
title: [Espanha] Ceuta, Marrocos e a utilização da classe trabalhadora como arma política
content: Da CNT, exigimos: • O esclarecimento das cerca de cem mortes ocorridas na fronteira. • A libertação dos detidos. • Transparência informativa total. • A libertação de todos os presos políticos das cadeias de Marrocos. • O fim da ditadura de Maomé VI. • O fim do apoio do governo espanhol a essa ditadura. • A proibição dos grupos parafascistas que parasitam cada crise política. • A reabertura dos passos fronteiriços de Ceuta e Melilha que estavam abertos antes da COVID. • A revogação da Lei de Estrangeiros. Queremos começar solidarizando-nos com os familiares e amigos de todas as pessoas falecidas e das famílias com pessoas presas. As recentes tensões entre os Estados espanhol e marroquino voltam a colocar Ceuta no centro de um conflito que, mais uma vez, se apresenta como uma simples questão de soberania nacional e de controle fronteiriço. No entanto, desde a CNT entendemos que essa abordagem oculta o verdadeiro problema e desvia a atenção de quem sofre as consequências: a classe trabalhadora. Tanto a de um lado quanto a do outro lado da fronteira. Os governos da Espanha e de Marrocos utilizam a fronteira como um instrumento de negociação política. O Estado marroquino emprega o controle dos fluxos migratórios como elemento de pressão diplomática, enquanto o Estado espanhol responde reforçando a militarização das fronteiras e endurecendo as políticas migratórias, “terceirizando” dessa forma essa política fronteiriça de mortes, fazendo concessões à ditadura de Maomé VI. Concessões como a legitimação de seu regime ditatorial, que conta com centenas de presos políticos, que pisoteia a legalidade internacional, como a validação da ocupação militar do Saara Ocidental, com seu rastro de violações dos Direitos Humanos. No meio dessa disputa entre Estados ficam milhares de pessoas trabalhadoras obrigadas a migrar pela repressão política, pela pobreza, pela precariedade, pela falta de oportunidades ou pelas consequências de um modelo econômico profundamente desigual. É essa desigualdade que, de fato, cria as fronteiras. Sem essa desigualdade, não há “fronteira”. Essa situação é aproveitada pela extrema direita que aponta as pessoas migrantes como causa dos problemas sociais. O fato de a chegada de pessoas migrantes se tornar um conflito internacional é uma decisão política do capital e dos governos que o administram. Nesse sentido, existe uma clara aliança de fato entre a extrema direita xenófoba, que defende os capitalistas e aponta os migrantes, e a ditadura do rei de Marrocos, ao qual, como está visto, pouco importa o seu próprio povo. Não é coincidência que há apenas alguns dias o ditador tenha batizado com o nome de “Donald Trump” uma autoestrada que pretende construir no Saara Ocupado. Saara ocupado, lembremos, com a ajuda militar que o Estado de Israel presta ao Estado marroquino. A classe dominante utiliza deliberadamente a escassez planejada de recursos públicos para confrontar uns trabalhadores com os outros. Enquanto se privatizam os serviços públicos, se limita o investimento social, empregando esse dinheiro em gasto militar, e se favorece a acumulação de lucros privados, alimenta-se o discurso de que o problema são aqueles que chegam em busca de uma vida melhor. Assim, desvia-se a responsabilidade de quem realmente concentra a riqueza e toma as decisões econômicas. As pessoas migrantes não são nossas inimigas. Também não o são os trabalhadores e trabalhadoras marroquinos, cuja exploração responde à mesma lógica que sofrem aqueles que trabalhamos no Estado espanhol. A competição entre trabalhadores não surge da migração, mas de um sistema econômico que precisa de mão de obra precarizada, sem direitos e facilmente explorável para pressionar para baixo as condições laborais do conjunto da classe trabalhadora. Nesse sentido, apoiamos as regularizações em massa que melhoram as condições de vida, que concedem direitos e que evitam essa mesma competição entre trabalhadores que tanto deseja a extrema direita. Como organização anarcossindicalista, rejeitamos tanto o nacionalismo espanhol quanto o marroquino. Nenhum Estado representa os interesses da classe trabalhadora. Frente àqueles que utilizam as fronteiras para defender interesses geopolíticos ou econômicos, reivindicamos a solidariedade internacional entre aqueles que vivem do nosso trabalho. A resposta não pode ser o fechamento de fronteiras, a militarização, nem o confronto entre povos. Também não pode consistir em aceitar que os serviços públicos permaneçam …

author: anred
title: Movilizan en todo el país contra la caída del Volver al Trabajo y la quita de ingresos a más de 929 mil trabajadores/as
content:
3/2/23. Piqueteros cortan de la 9 de julio en contra de las bajas de planes Potenciar Trabajo. Foto: Federico Imas

Más de 929 mil trabajadores y trabajadoras de comedores populares, reciclado urbano, tareas de cuidado comunitario y economía popular dejarán de percibir desde agosto el ingreso del programa Volver al Trabajo (ex Potenciar Trabajo). Frente a esta decisión del gobierno de Javier Milei, a través de su ministra de Capital Humano, Sandra Pettovello, organizaciones sociales, territoriales, sindicales y campesinas convocaron para este viernes 7 de agosto a una Jornada Nacional de Lucha con movilizaciones en todo el país. Las organizaciones denuncian que la medida representa un nuevo avance del ajuste sobre los sectores más empobrecidos y advierten que, además de afectar a casi un millón de familias, profundizará la caída del consumo y agravará la crisis social en los barrios populares. La convocatoria reúne a la Unión de Trabajadores y Trabajadoras de la Economía Popular (UTEP), el Frente de Lucha Piquetero, Territorios en Lucha, la Unidad de Organizaciones en Lucha, el Frente Barrial de la CTA, el Encuentro Socialista Antiimperialista, la Red de Organización Social Independiente y el Frente Social Nueva Independencia. Por ANRed.

La decisión del gobierno de Javier Milei – a través de su ministra de Capital Humano, Sandra Pettovello – de eliminar el ingreso mensual del programa Volver al Trabajo (ex Potenciar Trabajo) volverá a encontrar respuesta en las calles: este viernes 7 de agosto, organizaciones sociales, territoriales, campesinas y sindicales realizarán una Jornada Nacional de Lucha en todo el país para exigir la continuidad del programa y denunciar que la medida deja sin ingresos a más de 929 mil trabajadores y trabajadoras de la economía popular.

En un comunicado conjunto, las organizaciones advierten: «a partir de este mes de agosto, los 929.677 trabajadores y trabajadoras del programa Volver al Trabajo dejarán de percibir los $78.000 mensuales que reciben como reconocimiento por el enorme trabajo social y productivo que realizan en los barrios populares de todo el país. La medida afecta a cocineras y cocineros de comedores y merenderos, recicladores urbanos, trabajadores de limpieza en cientos de municipios, trabajadores de espacios públicos, trabajadoras de cuidado comunitario y miles de trabajadores y trabajadoras de la economía popular que sostienen tareas esenciales para sus comunidades», remarcan.

Marcha de los movimientos sociales, la CGT y las CTA “Paz, Pan, Tierra, Techo y Trabajo” el 7 de agosto de 2025. Foto achivo: Indymedia Argentina

El documento sostiene además que el impacto excede a quienes perciben el ingreso y alcanzará al conjunto de la economía popular: «además del impacto sobre casi un millón de familias, ésta decisión retirará de la economía real 72.514.806.000 de pesos cada mes, profundizando la crisis de las economías regionales y provocando una nueva caída del consumo«, alertaron.

Por ese motivo, convocaron a una amplia jornada de protesta en todo el país: «el 7 de agosto nos movilizamos en todo el país para defender el trabajo y exigir la continuidad de este ingreso», concluye la convocatoria.

La movilización se desarrollará en un contexto de creciente conflictividad social, marcado por las protestas contra el ajuste, los despidos, el deterioro del poder adquisitivo y los recortes en distintas áreas del Estado. En los últimos meses, las organizaciones sociales denunciaron un aumento sostenido de la demanda en comedores comunitarios y merenderos, mientras se reducen las políticas públicas destinadas a los sectores populares.

En este marco, la decisión de eliminar este ingreso también reabre el debate sobre el reconocimiento del trabajo comunitario y de la economía popular. Las organizaciones sostienen que las tareas que realizan —desde el sostenimiento de comedores hasta el reciclado urbano, el cuidado comunitario, la producción de alimentos y el mantenimiento de espacios públicos— constituyen actividades esenciales para millones de personas, especialmente en los barrios populares donde el Estado suele tener menor presencia.

Así, la Jornada Nacional de Lucha del 7 de agosto busca instalar que el conflicto trasciende la discusión sobre un programa social. Para las organizaciones convocantes, la eliminación del Volver al Trabajo forma parte de una política de ajuste más amplia impulsada por el gobierno de Javier Milei, que combina reducción del gasto social …

author: Kodao Productions
title: Did the Pasig Court Bypass the Labor Code?
content:
On July 9, National Capital Region’s (NCR) Regional Tripartite Wage and Productivity Board (RTWPB) announced that the first tranche of its Wage Order No. 27 would take effect on July 25. It grants a PHP 60 daily wage increase, followed by an additional P25 on January 20 next year, raising the minimum daily wage for non-agricultural workers in Metro Manila to P780.

The cumulative P85 increase is RTWPB’s largest single wage adjustment since its creation in 1989. While welcomed by most workers, however, the amount to them still falls far short of a living wage.

But even a mandated increase, it seems, is difficult for workers to receive. Before the wage hike could even fully take effect, its implementation was put on hold on the eve of the day most workers expect their monthly salaries.

Pasig Regional Trial Court (RTC) branch 152 issued a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) against the latest wage order last July 30, upon petition by two construction companies with at least hundreds of employees and billions of pesos in cumulative government infrastructure contracts.

Readycon Trading and Construction Corp., and R-II Builders, Inc. claimed the wage order would cause “grave injustice and irreparable injury” to their lucrative business, seeking relief from the Court against the alleged adverse effects of the wage order on their rights as businesses. The Court agreed, temporarily halting the wage increase until August 13, 2026.

The Pasig RTC also issued a status quo ante order a day before the wage hike was set to take effect, directing wage rates prior to the scheduled hike be maintained.

Labor secretary Francis Tolentino expressed “sadness” at the decision, pointing out that the wage hike order had undergone due deliberation and process by the Board process. He argued that workers who were already enjoying the increase prior to the Court order should not be made to reimburse the accrued amounts.

Various labor groups were unanimous in condemning the petitions and the Court decision, saying the latter has illegally arrogated unto itself a process that the Labor Code reserves exclusively for wage-setting bodies.

Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) chairperson Jerome Adonis slammed the orders do not make sense, describing it as an intervention against a hard-won wage adjustment affecting nearly three million workers in the region. He challenged DOLE’s Tolentino to immediately challenge the free order, pointing out that the petitioners should have appealed to National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC), as provided for under Article 126 of the Labor Code.

Adonis added the law prohibits trial courts from issuing temporary restraining orders or injunctions against the NWPC and the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards.

Labor groups Federation of Free Workers and SENTRO meanwhile has since filed urgent motions before the Pasig RTC, pushing for the immediate lifting of the TRO. The Nagkaisa workers’ coalition also held a protest rally before DOLE’s main office in Intramuros.

Other labor groups likewise challenged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to certify a legislated wage hike bill to prove his commitment to workers’ welfare.

No president since Corazon Aquino has approved a legislated wage hike, however. Succeeding presidents has only allowed regional wage boards to determine minimum wages in different regions. Minimum daily wage in the NCR stands at P755 while it is P436 in Muslim Mindanao.

The country’s labor laws also allow for exceptions in payment of minimum wages. Small businesses with 10 employees or less may apply for exceptions and may give their workers lower wages than the statutory salaries.

Economic think-tank IBON Foundation said the national average daily living wage must be P1,312 per day, or P28,426 per month. #

The post Did the Pasig Court Bypass the Labor Code? appeared first on Kodao Productions .

author: groundxero
title: #STOPKILLINGUS Protest at Jantar Mantar: Safai Karmacharis Accuses Centre of Concealing Sewer Deaths, Demands Parliamentary Inquiry
content:
“As Prime Minister, ackowledge this failure, make a national apology and take immediate action” , Safai Karmachari Andolan said in a memorandum to the Prime Minister .

New Delhi, August 4: Hundreds of sanitation workers from more than 10 states, families of those killed while cleaning sewers and septic tanks, Members of Parliament, students, writers, and civil society activists gathered at Jantar Mantar on Tuesday under the banner of the Safai Karmachari Andolan (SKA) — a movement for elimination of manual scavenging — to demand an end to sewer and septic tank deaths accusing the Union government of suppressing the actual number of deaths.

Organised under the slogan #STOPKILLINGUS , the protest condemned what SKA described as the government’s continued apathy towards the illegal practice of sending workers into sewers and septic tanks, resulting in preventable deaths. The organisation alleged that the Centre was attempting to disguise these deaths as ordinary workplace accidents instead of recognising them as consequences of an unlawful and caste-based practice.

Submitting a memorandum to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, SKA questioned the discrepancy between the government’s figures and its own documentation. It pointed out that while the Union government informed Parliament that 332 people had died in sewer and septic tank incidents between January 2021 and June 2026 , SKA’s documentation, supported by verified media reports, recorded 593 deaths between January 2021 and July 2026 .

“How did 593 deaths become 332? Where have you hidden the remaining 261 persons who were killed?” the memorandum asked, accusing the government of concealing deaths instead of preventing them.

According to SKA, its records show 47 deaths in 2021, 93 in 2022, 102 in 2023, 117 in 2024, and 121 in 2025. In 2026 alone , 113 people have already died between January and July, including 15 deaths in July.

The organisation argued that these fatalities cannot be described as accidents but are the result of illegally employing workers to enter hazardous sewers and septic tanks without adequate protection. It stated that such deaths violate Articles 14, 17, and 21 of the Constitution, relating respectively to equality before law, the abolition of untouchability, and the right to life.

SKA criticised the Union government’s NAMASTE Scheme, claiming that it had failed to prevent sewer and septic tank deaths despite being introduced to mechanise sanitation work and eliminate hazardous manual cleaning. It argued that the continuing rise in fatalities demonstrates the scheme’s failure to address the problem.

The protest also highlighted that SKA had earlier submitted memoranda to the Prime Minister on 25 March 2025 and 25 March 2026 , but had received no response.

On 1 August, during the ongoing Monsoon Session of Parliament, the organisation also submitted a memorandum to Members of Parliament, urging them to intervene.

Among its key demands, SKA called for:

A national apology from the Prime Minister acknowledging the government’s failure to stop sewer and septic tank deaths.

A Parliamentary Standing Committee inquiry into all sewer and septic tank deaths, with annual reports to Parliament on fatalities, prosecutions, compensation and rehabilitation.

A time-bound national plan to immediately eliminate sewer and septic tank deaths.

Recognition by the government that the NAMASTE Scheme has failed to prevent these deaths and requires fundamental changes.

Describing the deaths as “a matter of national shame”, the organisation maintained that ending manual scavenging and hazardous sanitation work requires political accountability, strict enforcement of existing laws, and the complete mechanisation of sewer and septic tank cleaning.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Se cumplió con alta adhesión el paro nacional docente en escuelas y universidades
content:
El paro nacional docente del 3 de agosto de 2026 registró una alta adhesión en escuelas y universidades de Argentina. La medida tuvo alto acatamiento y afectó el regreso a las aulas tras el receso invernal, agrupando reclamos por recomposición salarial, fondos nacionales y financiamiento universitario.

En Buenos Aires la marcha finalizó con un acto frente al Ministerio de Economía. Allí, la secretaria General de CTERA Sonia Alesso, describió la situación que viven los y las docentes y estudiantes por las políticas de Milei: “La frase que más se escucha es ¿Cuántas horas más puedo agarrar para ver si puedo pagar el alquiler y las expensas? Mi escuela está detonada. Esta gente que gobierna de espaldas al pueblo, que gobierna para los grandes empresarios, para el Fondo Monetario Internacional, no ve lo que vemos en la escuela todos los días”.

Además, convocó a marchar el 7 de agosto, el día de San Cayetano: “Los pibes con hambre, el aumento de los suicidios, las autolesiones, la situación de extrema pobreza, los comedores escolares rebalsados porque sacaron los comedores comunitarios. Por eso el día 7 vamos a estar marchando con las organizaciones sociales, con la iglesia, con el pueblo, diciendo paz, pan, techo y trabajo”.

Por otro lado, desde la Confederación de Trabajadores de la Educación calificaron como contundente la medida, por la alta participación que se verificó en la mayoría de las provincias. Los gremios universitario también fueron parte de esta jornada de paro nacional docente en reclamo del cumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario.

Octavio Miloni, secretario adjunto de la federación CONADU, que nuclea docentes universitarios, expresó: “Ponemos nuestras reivindicaciones dentro del contexto de las reivindicaciones de la docencia nacional, de la educación pública, de los trabajadores y trabajadoras de la educación privada también, porque no puede haber un país construyendo democracia sin el derecho a la educación que sea realmente efectivo”.

author: Alicia Griffiths
title: Melbourne tells Hanson where to go
content:
On the evening of 3 August, around 250 protesters gathered outside the Tower Hotel in Melbourne’s inner east. Inside, the far-right One Nation party was announcing its candidates for the Victorian state election to be held in November.

A large police presence was sent to protect the event and prevent protesters from getting near the venue. But our voices easily crossed the police lines, with the One Nation supporters being greeted with chants like, “Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” and “Pauline Hanson go to hell—take your racists there as well!” Party leader Pauline Hanson had slinked out through the adjoining bottle-o to avoid the protest.

The crowd heard speeches from a high school antifascist, a Swinburne student and a socialist involved in organising against Hanson when she first emerged as a political figure in the 1990s. The rally was called by the Campaign Against Racism and Fascism, which has been key to organising opposition to the far right in Melbourne over the last decade or more.

The protest was an important and much-needed display of opposition to Hanson, and something we will need more of in the lead-up to the state election. A campaign both in the streets and at the ballot box is needed to push back her racist, sexist, anti-worker agenda. Victorian Socialists candidate for the state seat of Hawthorn, Tess McEnearney, told the demonstration:

“What that looks like starts with each and every one of you here today—an anti-racist, anti-sexist left throughout Melbourne so big that One Nation can’t organise their campaign events without fear of protests, and so Pauline Hanson knows that if she wants to win this state election she is going to be facing a hell of a fight. And that we’re going to keep fighting and fighting and fighting until we win.”

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Locked Up and Criminalized: People on the Move Face a Broken System on Crete’s Shores
content:
Crete, Greece — People on the move arriving on Crete are held in makeshift facilities where they have no rights, as authorities freeze asylum registration while implementing the EU’s contested new Migration and Asylum Pact.

The abandoned Kitrenosis industrial complex sits along the highway connecting the cities of Rethymno and Heraklion, on Crete’s northern coast. The warehouses, disused for years, look out over a cliff that drops straight into the sea. Scattered across the outdoor lot are piles of objects hinting at a transient human presence: faded clothing, broken chargers, crumpled cigarette packs.

Crete has no dedicated reception system, and Kitrenosis is one of the stopgap solutions authorities have turned to after transferring people from the island’s southern shores, where boats arrive, to temporary holding sites in the north.

According to local media reports, the site was last used in December 2025, when it held more than 500 people. It has sat empty since, but inside one of the warehouses, traces of makeshift shelter remain. The space has no windows — a beam of sunlight creeping in through the gap in a broken gate is the only light inside the facility. The floor is littered with the remains of packaged food, half-empty water bottles, gym mats and flattened cardboard boxes.

In November 2025, the Italian organization Operazione Colomba published a report confirming the deplorable conditions at Kitrenosis and the island’s two other temporary facilities: the former exhibition center Agia, located about twenty minutes from downtown Chania, and the old refrigerated storage unit inside the port of Heraklion. The report found that all three sites lacked basic infrastructure and essentials, such as beds, showers, toilets, and clean clothing, and suffered from frequent overcrowding and a lack of privacy.

As of July 2026, all three facilities sit empty, a lull attributed to bad weather slowing arrivals. However, the latest data published by the independent organization Refugee Support Aegean puts the number of people who reached Crete in the first half of the year at roughly 8,500 — a figure confirming that the route from Libya to the island is now well-established, regardless of seasonal fluctuations.

Manufacturing an Emergency

“Crete has been a landing point for a long time. This isn’t new in the past year. What has changed is the political narrative,” Maria, an activist with the Chania-based migrant solidarity collective Steki Metanaston, told Unicorn Riot. As early as 2023, Refugee Support Aegean was already noting a rise in arrivals to Crete, flagging the complete absence of adequate reception infrastructure and procedures. By 2024, the same organization reported a further jump in landings, with more than 5,000 people reaching the island.

It was 2025, however, that saw the sharpest spike in absolute numbers. According to data released by Refugee Support Aegean, more than 20,000 people landed on Crete’s shores that year. This is a significant figure that made the island Greece’s main point of entry, but it needs context. The latest report published by the Asylum Information Database (AIDA), the Greek Council for Refugees and the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE) confirms that the route has become well-established, while also pointing to an overall drop in arrivals nationwide — down 21% from 2024 to 2025.

That figure has been almost entirely absent from political and media discourse. Instead, the raw number of arrivals hitting Crete’s coastline has been wielded as a propaganda tool by the conservative New Democracy government, first elected in 2019 and now serving its second term.

“The numbers are clear: arrivals are trending downward. What’s changing are the routes,” said Michalis Markodimitrakis, a researcher at the Hellenic Mediterranean University and a member of Thalassa of Solidarity, a Heraklion-based collective. “Greek authorities know this, as this redistribution has been happening for more than two years. But they’ve deliberately chosen to do nothing. Because if you do nothing, you can present the situation as a crisis, and in times of crisis, extreme measures are justified and meet little opposition.”

In July 2025, the Greek Parliament approved a measure suspending asylum claims for three months for people arriving from North African coasts. The decision, criticized by numerous independent organizations, was framed as a direct response to the rise in landings on Crete, which …

title: Stellungnahme aus autonom-antifaschistischer Sicht zu den Einlassungen am OLG Düsseldorf
content:
Stellungnahme aus autonom-antifaschistischer Sicht

Die vor dem OLG-Düsseldorf im sogenannten Budapest-Komplex angeklagten Antifaschist:innen haben am 14.07.2026 vor Gericht Aussagen zu einzelnen Anklagepunkten gemacht. Sie identifizierten sich auf Beweismaterial, distanzierten sich vom Vorwurf des versuchten Mordes und erklärten ihre antifaschistische Motivation. Das Statement von BASC (Budapest Antifascist Solidarity Committee) Jena versucht am 24.07.2026 diese Einlassungen einzuordnen.

Aus den Erfahrungen der radikalen Linken sagen wir:  Diese Einlassungen sind ein Fehler – politisch, strategisch und solidarisch.

Den seit Februar 2023 in Ungarn und Deutschland in Haft oder vor Gericht sitzenden Antifaschist:innen wird vorgeworfen, sich rund um den „Tag der Ehre“ in Budapest 2023 an Angriffen auf Faschisten beteiligt zu haben. Diese Verfahren sind ein Teil des Angriffs auf antikapitalistische linke Strukturen. Es geht um die Kriminalisierung von militantem Antifaschismus, um Einschüchterung, um internationale Zusammenarbeit der Repressionsapparate und darum, Antifaschist:innen mundtot zu machen. Es ist politische Justiz und es geht nicht um Wahrheitsfindung.

„Anna und Arthur halten’s Maul“ Das ist keine nostalgische Parole aus den Achtzigern, sondern die Basis unseres Verhälnisses zur Justiz. Der Grundsatz entstand aus der konkreten Erfahrung, dass Polizei, Staatsanwaltschaften und Geheimdienste jede Aussage verwerten: jede einzelne erscheint für sich vielleicht als harmlos, bietet der staatlichen Gegenseite aber Gelegenheit und Bausteine für weitere Angriffe auf uns. Staatliche Ermittlungen funktionieren wie ein Puzzle: Jedes Teilchen wird zum Gesamtbild, das von uns nicht kontrollierbar ist.

Politische Erklärungen zur Notwendigkeit antifaschistischer Gegenwehr sind etwas anderes als Angaben zu individuellen Aktivitäten. Wer sich jedoch auf Beweismaterial selbst identifiziert und inkriminierte Sachverhalte „richtig stellt“, liefert der Justiz Bausteine für weitere Verfolgungen und Verurteilungen – und erkennt die Zuständigkeit und die Verfahrensweisen der Justiz an.

Dass gleichzeitig der Vorwurf des versuchten Mordes zurückgewiesen wird, ändert daran nichts. Der Repressionsapparat – zu dem das Gericht gehört – behält sich die Bewertung und weitere Verwertung der Aussagen, auch und vor allem gegen weitere Personen, sowieso vor.

Besonders widersprüchlich ist die Situation, weil andere Antifaschist:innen wegen ihrer Aussageverweigerung in Beugehaft sitzen. Während sie (erneute) Inhaftierung in Kauf nehmen, um den Verfolgungsbehörden nicht zuzuspielen, tragen die Angeklagten in Düsseldorf aktiv zur Beweisaufnahme bei. Das sind nicht nur einfach „unterschiedliche individuelle Strategien“. Solidarität bedeutet auch, die eigenen individuellen Entscheidungen nach Möglichkeit zur Diskussion zu stellen. Nur so ließen sich die Folgen des eigenen Handelns für andere Verfahren und für die gesamte Struktur mitdenken.

Problematisch ist zudem die Hoffnung, die sogenannte „Beweiserhebung“ im Gerichtssaal kontrollieren zu können. Das Gericht ist nicht neutral. Es entscheidet selbst – wie auch die Staatsanwaltschaft – welche Aussagen protokolliert, juristisch verwertet und später gegen wen verwendet werden. Wer glaubt, mit Aussagen zu Tatvorwürfen ein politisches Zeichen setzen und die staatliche Beweisproduktion begrenzen zu können, überschätzt die eigene Kontrolle über das Verfahren.

Auch die Rede vom „staatlichen Versagen“ greift zu kurz. Staat und Sicherheitsbehörden haben rechte Gewalt nicht nur übersehen. Sie haben rechte Strukturen geschützt, finanziert, gelenkt, verharmlost und gleichzeitig Antifaschist:innen verfolgt. Das ist kein Betriebsunfall, sondern besitzt politische Kontinuität. Der Staat trägt die Tendenz zum Faschismus als Möglichkeit für den Umgang mit Krisen in sich – er braucht die Faschisten. Sich gegenüber genau diesen Institutionen erklärend zu rechtfertigen, führt daher in die falsche Richtung.

Natürlich stehen Menschen unter enormem Druck. Haft, drohende lange Strafen und jahrelange Verfahren können die (vereinzelten) Betroffenen überfordern. Darauf zielt die Repression. Verständnis für die persönliche Lage bedeutet aber nicht, diese Entscheidungen politisch richtigzuheißen. Gerade in solchen Situationen braucht es den Halt eines klaren kollektiven Grundsatzes.

Para la Cancillería de Brasil, “Milei es un capanga de Trump”. La caracterización es harto justificada. Pero el dueño del chancho, Trump, quiere tomar por asalto a Brasil por medio de una injerencia militar contra el pretexto del “terrorismo”, o sea, una usurpación de la soberanía estatal de Brasil, así como por medio de una guerra comercial y sanciones financieras, la intromisión en el proceso electoral del país vecino y el apoyo sin restricciones a la ultraderecha y al fascismo brasileño. La histeria fascista de Milei, sobre todo, se encuentra motivada por la necesidad de que el Tesoro norteamericano salga, por tercera o cuarta vez, al rescate de las finanzas libertarias. El capanga argentino teme haber perdido el respaldo del Norte y tener que devaluar. Así como Donald Trump no consigue imponer sus exigencias en las guerras criminales en las que ha empeñado a Estados Unidos, Milei está llevando a Argentina a una bancarrota industrial y financiera, cuando comienza su cuarto año de gobierno.

Por Política Obrera.


Para la Cancillería de Brasil, “Milei es un capanga de Trump”, según informa la prensa del país vecino. La caracterización es harto justificada. Pero el dueño del chancho, Trump, quiere tomar por asalto a Brasil por medio de una injerencia militar contra el pretexto del “terrorismo”, o sea, una usurpación de la soberanía estatal de Brasil, así como por medio de una guerra comercial y sanciones financieras, la intromisión en el proceso electoral del país vecino y el apoyo sin restricciones a la ultraderecha y al fascismo brasileño. El gobierno brasileño se ha visto obligado a negar la visa a tres funcionarios de Washington, que se habían arrogado la tarea de ‘supervisar’ a los organismos electorales de Brasil. Itamaraty, por otro lado, entiende que Lula es “un peso pesado de la política mundial”, que no debe cruzarse con “un peso pluma”. Pero si lo que importa, por cierto, no es el chancho sino quien le da de comer, el patrón de la estancia, Donald Trump, está empeñado en restablecer la hegemonía internacional del imperialismo norteamericano por medio de la guerra y, en especial, en su patio trasero. No cabe, entonces, rehuir una confrontación, sino desarrollarla en forma consecuente y apuntar a la cabeza mediante la movilización de masas.


Los sarcasmos de la diplomacia brasileña no constituyen una respuesta política a lo que es una ofensiva continental del imperialismo. Milei tiene agendado hacerse presente en la ceremonia de traspaso del mando presidencial a Keiko Fujimori, en Perú, y al de Adalberto de la Espriella, en Colombia, junto a toda la tropa fascista latinoamericana. Las reacciones diplomáticas de las cancillerías no alcanzan para derrotar esta ofensiva. Lula rehúsa apoyarse en una movilización popular debido a sus propios lazos con la burguesía local, que puebla el gabinete del Planalto. Esa movilización sólo partirá de una iniciativa independiente; el colombiano Gustavo Petro pagó caro su inmovilismo en cuanto a un llamado a la intervención de las masas.


Que Milei sea un capanga de Trump tiene otra implicancia, a saber, que Argentina ha caído al status de un protectorado de hecho. La coalición libertaria, compuesta por las fracciones internas de LLA, el PRO y numerosos gobernadores, no ha denunciado la provocación fascista de su candidato a la reelección. Tampoco ha habido un pronunciamiento ni tentativa de pronunciamiento en el Congreso; la agenda se establece en la Comisión de Labor Parlamentaria, que integran todos los partidos. Aunque no celebren los disparates del loco de atar, nadie tiene la intención de ponerle un chaleco de fuerza. El ‘flamante’ Jefe de Gabinete, Diego Santilli, aplaudió los insultos de Milei a Lula y a los miembros de la Suprema Corte de Brasil. El gobierno de Argentina se reduce a una banda de ‘hooligans’.

title: A new hunting season has been declared (pt. 2), or the normalisation of fascism
content:
On the 16th of July, at the invitation of Marco Rubio and the US State Department, representatives of over 60 countries

gathered

 to hear Rubio

annonce

 that “the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left”, wherever it might show itself, for “the left”, in its many incarnations, is the implacable enemy of the “West” and its civilization.


This is a distinctive and unique evil.  It has always been driven by a hatred above all else, a hatred for civilization itself.  It is a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good.  It is perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.  This is what radical leftism is.  It may wear various different slogans and ideologies across place and time.  They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist.  But the fundamental character is always the same.  It’s always the same. 


It is a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice and liberation, an overwhelming need to tear down what greater men have built, to wreck what is beautiful and what is right on behalf of people who are only filled with ugliness and have nothing else to offer the world.  Through violence and through terror, they once again seek to impose their ugliness on all of us.  The old dogma was wrong.  The old dogma was wrong; none of this is driven by idealism.  It is not utopian.  In fact, it is the opposite. 


If the threat comes from “within”, the “left” is nevertheless “transnational”, with financial and ideological support coming from countries such as Iran and

Cuba

. (“Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory. … It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance. … Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.” –  from

Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism

The report blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”) In other words, if the “indigenous left” of the USA is fundamentally a threat, it is ultimately a foreign, un-American threat which must be dealt with on a global scale through the construction of a new, “anti-leftist” global order.


After Rubio’s intervention, the stage was given to the White House deputy chief of staff, Steven Miller, whose

words

Left-wing terrorism always ends in bloodshed, misery, and suffering.  It only can travel in one direction.  There’s no point at which the left-wing terrorist is satisfied with his gains and ceases progressing.  Inevitably, left to run its course, it always becomes a gulag.  It always becomes the mass imprisonment of political enemies, the stripping of their rights and freedoms, inflicting immense pain, humiliation, suffering in order to establish complete and total control – control through psychological and physical and actual terror.  And we have to understand that that is the scope and the extent of the threat that we face.

content:
hierophagy

:

and my take today is that framing misogynistic writing as an “inability to write female characters” subconsciously takes away most of the blame, implying that women are an alien creature compared to men and that it is no fault of the writer because it’s out of their skill set. it’s not an inability, not a lack of expertise, it’s the simple refusal to consider women as individual people and give them the same depth and grace that comes easily to the writer when they write male characters. it’s not that christopher nolan, stephen king, james cameron (and frankly anyone using the argument, both professional and hobbyist; yes, that includes fanfic writers) etc can’t write women, it’s that they just won’t. at that point in time it is a conscious decision driven by the laziness to unpack their misogynistic biases, and should be addressed as such

author: Mosha Folger
title: Sanirajak man sentenced to four and a half years for sex crimes
content:
After a series of delays, Simeonie Issigaitok has received a four-and-a-half year sentence in a federal penitentiary for sexually touching children under the age of 16.

Court staff brought the 73-year-old Sanirajak man from into an Iqaluit courtroom Tuesday in a wheelchair. Through an interpreter, he listened expressionless, occasionally nodding his head, as Justice Christian Lyons read his sentence.

“Vulnerability of Inuit children and, in particular Inuit girls, is demonstrated by the persistent and troublingly high per capita rate of child sexual abuse in Nunavut,” Lyons said. “A problem that Mr. Issigaitok has repeatedly and substantially contributed to for decades.”

Issigaitok pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of sexual interference. The first offence occurred in Sanirajak sometime between 1987 and 1989. Issigaitok assaulted a girl in her early teens at her home while her parents were asleep.

The second incident occurred in April 2021. Issigaitok was captured on security video during a community event touching a boy while he was seated with a group of children.

On Tuesday, Lyons said aggravating factors included Issigaitok’s history of convictions for sex crimes dating back to  which dates back to 1988, his 2014 designation as a dangerous offender, and that his victims were Inuit children.

He also said that he considered the fact that Issigaitok attended residential school, where he was sexually abused, a mitigating factor, as well as Issigaitok’s guilty plea, which meant the victims did not have to testify.

Another mitigating factor was that one of the crimes occurred before the first of his 27 lifetime convictions. Therefore, the court could treat it as a first offense.

“This is attenuated somewhat by the fact that Mr. Issigaitok was abusing other children during the period of the offense and had committed a serious sexual assault a few years prior, for which he was sentenced in 1997,” Lyons said.

Crown prosecutors had sought a 10-year sentence, while defence lawyer Alan Regel argued that his sentence should be for time served in jail while his case worked its way through the legal system. Judges usually credit defendants with one and a half days for every day they spend in pre-trial custody. That means Regal was asking for a sentence of about 21 months.

Lyons sentenced Issigaitok to three years for the crime committed in 1988 and one and a half years for the crime committed in 2021.

Issigaitok will remain at the Aaqqigiarvik Correctional Healing Facility in Iqaluit while he awaits his transfer to a federal penitentiary to serve the two years and nine months left in his sentence.

The sentencing saw two delays. In June, Lyons delayed the proceeding to allow time for one victim to submit a statement. In July, Issigaitok was medevaced to Ottawa because of respiratory problems.

There was one more delay, of about an hour, on Tuesday. The scheduled court interpreter was not in town, and court staff needed to videoconference a new one.

author: Equality Now
title: Justice delayed across borders: What the Tate cases reveal about the cost of system failure
content:
For years, women have come forward with allegations of sexual violence against Andrew and Tristan Tate. Investigations have unfolded in Romania. Civil proceedings have taken place in the United Kingdom. Criminal charges now span multiple jurisdictions. Most recently, the brothers were jailed in the United States while awaiting extradition to the UK, where they will face charges including rape, trafficking for sexual exploitation, assault and other serious offences. They deny all allegations.

Taken together, these developments should represent a significant step toward accountability. Instead, they raise an unsettling question:

Why does it take allegations across multiple countries, years of investigations and extensive public evidence before justice systems begin to catch up?

The answer is linked to the numerous and persistent failures of the institutions responsible for delivering justice and protecting the most vulnerable from exploitation.

Accountability should not depend on crossing borders

The allegations against the Tate brothers, known for their social media presence , have involved conduct said to have occurred across different countries over many years, creating overlapping investigations spanning multiple jurisdictions, and resulting in lengthy legal processes.

Often in trafficking cases, survivors have to navigate different legal systems, evidentiary standards and repeated delays while proceedings unfold; the multiple cases involving the Tate brothers are no different.

In Romania, prosecutors allege that the brothers formed an organised criminal group that recruited and exploited women, including through methods of psychological pressure and control, and have charged them with human trafficking and rape.

In the United Kingdom, prosecutors have authorised charges including rape, actual bodily harm and arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Whether perpetrated across physical and digital spaces or across national borders, exploitation exists on a continuum , and justice systems should be equipped to respond accordingly and in a timely manner. Yet too often, laws, institutions and enforcement mechanisms remain siloed, creating gaps that traffickers and exploiters can exploit.

International human rights law already provides a framework for tackling these crimes. The Palermo Protocol defines trafficking as the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of persons through threats or use of force, coercion, abduction, deception, abuse of a position of vulnerability or other prohibited means for the purpose of exploitation and calls on States to work together to prevent trafficking, protect survivors, investigate offences and prosecute perpetrators.

The recent extradition proceedings in the Tate cases demonstrate that international cooperation is possible. But they also expose how long survivors may be forced to wait before justice systems work together effectively.

Understanding patterns of systematic exploitation

As outlined in this in-depth piece by The New Yorker, perhaps the most disturbing aspect of these cases involving the Tate brothers is the consistency of the alleged methods used to violate and traffic a number of individuals.

From allegations of calculated recruitment, coercive control, financial exploitation, to sexual violence, these alleged acts have been highlighted as patterns as part of an organised business model rather than isolated crimes.

Recognising these patterns is important to defining the crime as the human rights violation it is,  because trafficking rarely resembles the stereotypes many people still imagine.

Trafficking can take many forms and humans can be trafficked for many reasons. Survivors can be trafficked for sexual exploitation, forced labour, domestic servitude, or forced criminality, among other things. Often these forms of exploitation are interconnected, and many survivors have experienced multiple forms of exploitation once trafficked.

Under international human rights law, trafficking is defined by its exploitative purpose, and while people of all genders can experience trafficking, women and girls are disproportionately affected by trafficking for sexual exploitation.

author: rti_admin
title: Selective Ritual Reform and Buddhist Marriage Among Ambedkarites in Odisha
content:
Abstract: Marriage rituals in South Asia have historically reinforced caste and gender hierarchies. Within contemporary Ambedkarite Buddhist communities in Odisha, debates over “mixed marriages” frequently centre on visible Hindu practices such as Brahmin priests, sindur , and the mangalsutra . Drawing on Ambedkarite social media discussions, wedding practices, B. R. Ambedkar’s writings, and anthropological studies of marriage, this article argues that such critiques are often selective. While many Ambedkarites reject Brahmanical symbols, they continue practices such as the baraat , engagement rituals such as Nadia Dhara ( ring ceremonies), status matching in partner selection, and competitive wedding display. These practices reproduce caste, gender, and status hierarchies in new forms. This article argues that Ambedkarite Buddhist marriage remains an evolving social project. Its transformative potential depends on changing the social relations that organise marriage, not simply replacing Brahmanical symbols. It calls on Dalit Bahujan communities to reimagine Buddhist marriage as an ethical practice grounded in equality, solidarity, and collective uplift.

Introduction: Hindu marriage has often been understood as a religious and soteriological event embedded within broader moral and ritual frameworks (Harman, 1987). At the same time, marriage has historically operated as a key social institution through which caste, gender, and hierarchy are regulated and reproduced (Ambedkar, 1916/1979). As Ambedkar argued, the endurance of caste rests significantly on the regulation of marriage, particularly through endogamy and the control of women’s mobility and sexuality. Rituals surrounding marriage are therefore not incidental cultural practices but central mechanisms through which social order is maintained, reproduced, and publicly displayed.

However, marriage also carries the potential for transformation, especially within communities committed to equality and social justice. In the context of Ambedkarite marriage, it becomes a critical site for practising dignity, equality, and mutual respect. At the same time, inherited caste and patriarchal structures can continue to persist in new forms within intimate relationships. It is within this tension between reproduction and transformation that the significance of marriage must be understood. For Ambedkar, challenging caste required transforming both political institutions and everyday social practices that maintain caste boundaries.

The mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956 formed part of this broader social project. Conversion signified a rejection of Brahmanical religious authority, and an embrace of an ethical framework based on equality and rationality (Ambedkar, 1957). Yet the question of how marriage is practised within Ambedkarite communities remains open.

In recent years, debates within Ambedkarite circles in Odisha have increasingly focused on what many describe as “mixed marriages.” The term refers to weddings that identify themselves as Buddhist while simultaneously incorporating rituals and practices associated with Hindu traditions. These include the presence of Brahmin priests, Sanskrit mantras, fire rituals, dowry exchanges, and engagement or practices such as kanyadaan and the symbolic “gift of the daughter.” In many marriages, families also continue to rely on astrology through kundali matching and the selection of an auspicious muhurat, practices that shape ideas of compatibility, timing, and ritual legitimacy. Ambedkarite activists and commentators often criticise these practices because they reproduce Brahmanical structures of caste, thereby weakening the emancipatory potential of Buddhist marriage. Such critiques frequently draw upon Ambedkar’s analysis of caste, endogamy, and the social regulation of marriage, and emphasise that ritual reform is central to the broader project of annihilating caste.

However, contemporary discussions also reveal an important asymmetry. While explicitly Hindu ritual elements are strongly criticised, other practices common within Ambedkarite weddings receive little scrutiny. One such practice is the baraat, the celebratory procession in which the groom travels to the bride’s home accompanied by music, dancing, and relatives. This article examines why certain rituals become objects of critique while others remain normalised within Ambedkarite communities in Odisha. I argue that critiques of “mixed marriage” tend to focus on …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Media community faces killings, weaponization of laws under Marcos Jr.
content:
A placard highlighting a call to stop the attacks against community journalists placed on the floor during a protest action at the UP College of Media and Communication on May 2, 2025, a day before World Press Freedom Day. Photo by Alex Culla/Bulatlat

“Protecting press freedom is a shared responsibility. Without it, the public’s right to know and the foundations of democratic society are at risk.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — Four years since Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assumed the presidency, press freedom violations continue.

Eleven journalists and media workers were killed under his administration, according to the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP), although two of them were initially reported as not work-related. The latest case happened in May when Nestor Micator , radio broadcaster of D’Empire Radio, was shot dead by an unidentified assailant in Malidegao town which is under the Special Geographic Area of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

Community journalist RJ Nichole Ledesma was also killed during a military operation in Toboso, Negros Occidental, in April. He was reportedly in the area doing community work. However, the Philippine Army stressed that he was a New People’s Army (NPA) combatant, a claim assailed by media and human rights organizations.

Roxas City-based broadcaster Jay Lavapiez , meanwhile, encountered a near-death experience after he was ambushed in June.

In May, the Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFoMS) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) for what they called stronger collaboration and case buildup efforts.

PTFoMS also signed a MOA with the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) last year. Aside from advocating to expedite the resolution of cases, the agreement would establish a rapid response mechanism, psychosocial assistance for victims, and capacity-building and prevention for media workers.

The Philippine National Police (PNP), in partnership with PTFoMS and other government agencies, launched the PNP Media Security Vanguards program aimed at enhancing the safety and security of media practitioners.

Read: Media groups decry harassment of journalists, activist during protest

The NUJP, however, stressed that the State has failed to bring to justice the masterminds behind these killings. Among them were the murders of Renato Blanco, Percival Mabasa , Cresenciano Bundoquin , Juan Jumalon, Juan Dayang , Erwin Segovia , Noel Samar , and Julito Calo . “While four suspects behind two of these killings have been arrested, no mastermind has been brought to justice,” NUJP said in an earlier statement.

Read: Philippines remains dangerous for journalists

The group backed the proposal of Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and Opinion Irene Khan for the Philippine government to establish a “Special Prosecutor” for crimes against journalists and human rights defenders.

On the other hand, the local press freedom group also monitored the filing of cases against journalists and media workers. Aside from libel and cyberlibel, the Data Privacy Act and unjust vexation were reportedly weaponized as a usual form of retaliation against the media community.

Bacolod-based journalist Marchel Espina surrendered to the authorities upon learning that there was an arrest warrant issued against her for an unjust vexation case which stemmed from an opinion piece published in SunStar Cebu in 2024 when she was still the editor-in-chief.

The same charges were filed against Negros Occidental-based journalist Erwin Delilan in the first quarter of 2026 after the complainants got annoyed with his Binalaybay —a term used for Hiligaynon poems—commentaries on social media. Delilan was arrested twice prior to posting bail.

Lavapiez and his wife, India , who is also a radio broadcaster, also faced multiple cyberlibel cases filed by local officials. In August 2025, the Sangguniang Bayan of Sigma declared the two personas non grata for allegedly disseminating false and misleading information.

Cases of alleged violation of the Data Privacy Act were also filed against the late DZRH reporter Misael Gonzales Jr. after publishing the details indicated in an arrest warrant, as well as iFM Cagayan de Oro News Director Menzie Montes for posting screenshots of her conversation with a local official.

The NUJP monitored 15 libel and cyberlibel cases and 17 other forms of judicial harassment so far. These formed part of the overall …

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Inside Greece’s Refugee Camps, Gender-Based Violence Is Built Into the System
content:
Ritsona, Greece — Since 2022, the German collective Rosa Rolling Safespace has been providing a mobile safe space for women living in refugee camps around Athens. Their work shows that gender-based violence in these settings is not incidental but structural, a direct product of European and Greek migration policies.


Ritsona is a small town about 47 miles north of Athens. Driving through the surrounding countryside, it is hard to miss a sprawling cluster of gray containers encircled by barbed wire, surveillance cameras, and heavy metal gates monitored by police. It is one of the largest refugee camps in mainland Greece — according to

the latest data

 released by the Greek Ministry of Migration and Asylum, it has a nominal capacity of nearly 3,000 people.


Around the camp, hills and wind turbines stretch as far as the eye can see, occasionally interrupted by some industrial facilities breaking the monotony of the empty countryside. Once a week, however, a small dusty lot a few hundred meters from the camp’s main entrance comes to life.


Rosa Rolling Safespace setting up outside Ritsona camp. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


It is a Wednesday, and around midday two white vans appear at the far end of the long road running alongside the Ritsona camp. They park in the lot, and a group of about ten volunteers immediately get to work setting up a safe space for the women living inside.


Within half an hour, tables with hot and cold drinks, sewing machines, books, and children’s toys appear under a gazebo and a large yellow tent. The back of the larger van swings open, revealing a mobile medical clinic stocked with pads, tampons, and other essential supplies.


Medical truck brought to Ritsona camp by Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Medical truck with supplies brought to Ritsona camp by Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


Sewing machines getting set up at Ritsona camp by volunteers from Rosa Rolling Safespace. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


The volunteers are part of

Rosa Rolling Safespace

, a self-funded German collective that has been operating in mainland Greece since 2022.


“The project started from the understanding that women experience different forms of violence,” said Ari, one of the volunteers. “Everyone who migrates is subjected to structural violence, but being a woman in this context adds specific layers.”


Every week, the vans travel between the camps of Ritsona, Malakasa, Oinofyta, and Thiva, all located in the greater Athens area. The collective provides mobile medical care, a community space, and a dedicated children’s area.


Ari explains that many women in the camps have no points of reference and often lack the time and energy to seek help when they need it. “The medical truck and the community space work together precisely for this reason,” she said. “Women come every week, sit down, talk with us. Our goal is to build trust, so they know there is a safe space they can always come back to if they need help.”


Rosa Rolling Safespace operates from a parking lot outside the camp partly as a deliberate political choice. “We don’t want to support this oppressive system,” said Ari. “We reject the way the European asylum system is designed and the effects it has on people. We don’t want to be complicit in it.”


Rosa Rolling Safespace set up outside Ritsona camp. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.


But it is also a bureaucratic necessity. In 2020, the Greek government introduced

mandatory registration

 for organizations seeking to operate inside the camps. The process — costly and discretionary — effectively pushed out most independent groups, forcing them to work on the margins of the system. The result has been a double vacuum: fewer services for camp residents, and less independent monitoring of what happens inside.


This is not an accident. The current structure of refugee camps in Greece took shape with the EU’s

hotspot approach

, introduced in 2015 in response to arrivals by sea from Turkey. Originally designed as spaces for rapid identification and processing on the Aegean islands, hotspots gradually became containment facilities. 


In 2016, the

closure of borders

 by Macedonia, Croatia, and Slovenia left tens of thousands of people stranded in Greece, giving authorities a pretext to set up what were framed as emergency structures but have since become permanent.


The

EU-Turkey deal of March 2016 …
