author: Mekong Review 2
title: No one owes you a living Kirsten Han
content:
Singapore declares itself a “pro-family” country, but there’s a gap between ideal and reality. Credit: Singapore Stock Photos / Unsplash Unease: Life in Singapore Families Teo You Yenn Ethos Books: 2026 . On the surface, Singapore gleams. It’s wealthy, orderly, safe. The trains (generally) run on time, the amenities are plentiful, and the tiny city-state punches above its weight in international rankings to do with governance and education. Singapore is regularly brought up by policy wonks and politicians around the world—and across the political spectrum—as a model to learn from. The government enthusiastically proclaims itself to be “pro-family”, gearing policies towards supporting (heterosexual) Singaporeans with getting married and having children. What’s not to like?

Everything sounds great on paper. Yet, through years of research and lengthy interviews with close to a hundred parents, sociologist Teo You Yenn uncovers a different reality: “Everyday life is hectic and tense; life is stable but not quite secure; there is a pathway to follow but it does not always seem right; family is everything but family life feels off-kilter.” There is, she observes, a “sense of unease” that sits in the hearts of families in Singapore, regardless of their socioeconomic background.

Teo’s previous book, This Is What Inequality Looks Like—an ethnographic study of low-income households in Singapore—became a national bestseller when it hit the shelves in 2018. It pushed Singaporeans to look beyond rhetoric about “uplifting the poor” and instead consider inequality as a nationwide condition from which none of us can be extricated. With Unease: Life in Singapore Families, Teo directs attention to quotidian family life and once again prompts Singaporeans to reflect on the nature of the water we swim in.

Setting out to understand how parents navigate the much coveted but often elusive work–life balance, Teo finds that it isn’t basic childcare that occupies the most real estate in parents’ minds—it’s education. “Education systems or policies are rarely considered, by scholars or policymakers, as a source of work-life conflict; yet, my research shows that education has become a big component of ‘care labour’,” she writes. “Contemporary demands on parenting go well beyond baths and burps and fevers and sleeplessness, to supervision and nagging and strategising and conflicts of an entirely different, arguably more stress-inducing, level.”

Everyone in Singapore knows of the “kiasu parent”. Translated from Hokkien, to be ‘kiasu’ means to be afraid to lose, or lose out. The kiasu parent is obsessed with ensuring their kid keeps up with, if not outstrips, the rest of their cohort. The kiasu parent studies school rankings as if they contain the meaning of life and plots to get their offspring into the best option. The kiasu parent harasses teachers for progress reports and even demands extra homework. The kiasu parent, keeping tabs on what other (kiasu) parents are doing, signs their sprog up for extra tuition in all subjects… and also for piano, swimming, and ballet.

This archetype of the kiasu parent is often the butt of jokes—a beast to be reckoned with, but one we roll our eyes at. Government officials evoke their spectre when speaking of the need for a “mindset shift”, implying that the problems of a pressure-cooker education system stem from individual attitudes. Things would surely change if only all these parents could just stop being so kiasu.

Teo has no interest in lecturing parents. She’s much more invested in the structures within which Singaporean parents operate. Kiasu parents do not simply emerge, fully-formed, from Singapore’s diminishing rainforests; if they’re terrified of losing out, something must be making them feel like competitors in the first place. And individual parents have neither the clout nor capacity to shape the arena and dictate the rules. That can only come from something bigger and more powerful: government policies, institutional processes and procedures, social conditions that everyone has to respond or adapt to.

Education is a high-stakes game in Singapore. Although there have been shifts, over the years, away from a hyper-focus on academic results, the practices of scoring and sorting are still prevalent. Exam results still determine one’s ability to enter certain schools, access particular opportunities, or obtain qualifications from tertiary institutions—all of which can have a material impact …

author: Mekong Review 2
title: The way of the sword Simon Rowe
content:
A samurai with a katana . Credit: Nymphalyda Musashi: The Novel (Books One to Three) Eiji Yoshikawa, translated by Alexander Bennett Tuttle Publishing: 2026 . On a frigid January morning, I boarded a train from the samurai castle town of Himeji and journeyed west into the mountainous hinterland of Okayama Prefecture. Changing to a one-carriage diesel locomotive at the small town of Sayo, I continued on through long tunnels and deep valleys until, at a lonely siding, the train stopped. The sole passenger, I disembarked at the village of Miyamoto.

“Miyamoto Village lay silent,” writes Eiji Yoshikawa in the early pages of Musashi: The Novel, his sprawling samurai epic about the wandering swordsman, Miyamoto Musashi, whose search for life’s meaning takes him through the deep valleys, castle towns, and snow-bounded hinterlands of western Japan. Miyamoto Village did indeed lie silent as I trudged towards it—its traditional homesteads all but submerged in fresh snow, wooden shrines and temples groaning under the weight of the drifts.

Readers needn’t travel so far for a taste of rural Japanese antiquity. While Yoshikawa, who completed Musashi in 1939, has done those hard yards and spared you the trouble, it is Alexander Bennett, an Antipodean martial artist and scholar, whose translation of the original manuscript in its entirety now gives international readers access to the atmosphere and thrills of Japan’s greatest samurai tale.

This new unabridged version is no light undertaking. Told over three volumes, it comes in at a hefty 1,696 pages. But there are plenty of reasons to make the commitment. For one, it is a rollicking yarn with a cast of colourful characters. The settings are ever-changing; from rural hamlets, snowy mountain passes, and bamboo forests, to hectic city streets with brothels, boozy taverns, temples, and dojos, the reader is whisked along at a lively clip. This is feudal Japan in the early Edo Period—about 400 years ago—a time when the country was transitioning from civil war to an era of peace, order, and artistic freedom. Alongside martial arts, Yoshikawa also gives us cultural practices such as tea ceremonies, calligraphy, and flower arrangement—arts which samurai of yore engaged in to strengthen their mental discipline and build character.

Miyamoto Musashi was a real person who lived from 1594 to 1645. His name is known to all Japanese—if not as ‘Kensei (sword saint)’, then as a folk hero whose legendary strength and skill are still revered. Kids emulate his Niten Ichi-ryū (Two Heavens as One) style of swordsmanship with Chanbara foam swords; brands of kitchen knives, health supplements, home security systems, and even automotive parts are named after him. My local hardware store is called “Musashi”.

Yoshikawa has been instrumental in all of this, of course, popularising historical fiction with his reimagining of the lives of famous samurai figures in works like Taiko and The Heike Story—inspiring countless movies, TV dramas, and manga. Bennett’s new translation of Musashi—more than four decades after Charles S. Terry’s version—is sure to extend that popularity to an international readership.

Bennett is aptly qualified. A resident of Kyoto who lectures on Japanese history and culture at a university in Osaka, he holds multiple black belts in kendo, iaido, and naginata, among others. He is also editor-in-chief of Kendo World, an English-language publication on Japanese martial arts. So, when he states in his introduction that Musashi is “more than just a tale; it’s a meaningful interpretation of Japan’s cultural and philosophical heritage”, I’m inclined to believe him.

Musashi’s plot is epic but not unwieldy, charting the legendary swordsman’s physical and spiritual journey across the three volumes, each named after Godai (五大), the five great elements of Japanese Buddhist philosophy which represent the universe.

Musashi: Book One – Earth, Water and Fire begins on the corpse-strewn plains of Sekigahara, the site of Japan’s most decisive battles between the Eastern and Western warring states. We are introduced to the teenage ruffian, Takezō, and his hapless childhood friend, Matahachi, who, seeking adventure and glory, have sadly ended up on the losing side.

The two friends escape. Returning to Miyamoto Village, Takezō meets Takuan, a monk who forces him to take a long hard look at himself:

“You have natural brawn and a dash of boldness, but you’re woefully lacking in brains. You’ve mastered …

author: Mekong Review 2
title: Philippines: the dramedy Sol Iglesias
content:
Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. Credit: Juergen Nowak / Shutterstock.com Beyond Geopolitics: The Philippines in the New Marcos Era Edited by Cleo Anne A. Calimbahim and Björn Dressel ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute: 2026 . When I need to explain the collapse of the ‘UniTeam’ alliance between President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr and his vice-president, Sara Duterte, I like to use a—ahem—highly sophisticated political paradigm of ‘Team Kadiliman (Darkness) versus Team Kasamaan (Evil)’. The reference is to a video of a hapless Harry Roque, the former Rodrigo Duterte spokesperson and current fugitive, rallying his former boss’s supporters outside Congress. In the clip, he says, in Filipino, that the battle is no longer between the Dutertes and the Marcoses. Instead, he goes, “it’s a fight between the forces of darkness versus the forces of…?” He pauses expectantly.

“Evil!” the crowd shouts innocently.

“The forces of good!” he corrects them.

To my delight, Carmel V. Abao references the same viral video in her chapter, ‘The Marcos Jr. Administration: From Populism to Reformism?’, in , edited by Cleo Anne A. Calimbahin and Björn Dressel. Abao recounts the twists and turns of Marcos Jr’s presidency until the midterms in 2025, helping readers navigate the workings of these fractious elite coalitions.To read the rest of this article, and to access all Mekong Review content, please subscribe. If you are an existing subscriber, please login to your account to continue reading.

Being a Singapore government think tank, the tends to publish on relatively timely issues, quickly. For example, they published Games, Changes and Fears: The Philippines from Duterte to Marcos Jr.—on the transition from Duterte to Marcos Jr—in 2024, just two years after the presidential election. Drawing on the expertise of mainly academics, Beyond Geopolitics serves a middle audience sandwiched between the needs of political operators, who need analysis fresh out of the news cycle, and historians, who are utterly unhurried and probably wouldn’t mind waiting a few decades for proper perspective. Taken together, the book helps make sense of developments in the past years and months across different fields, helpful for watchers of Philippine politics to fill gaps in their knowledge of major issues. It’s a hefty eighteen-chapter collection, so there’s practically something for everyone.

Jan Carlo Punongbayan tells us about the economy at midterm: plummeting growth, weak consumption, inflationary pressure on food and energy, slow investment. He’d written a book dispelling economic myths about the administration of Ferdinand Marcos Sr—the ousted dictator and father of the current president—so he also shows us signs of “Marcosian” rehabilitation like Kadiwa stores, Masagana rice self-sufficiency, and, crucially, the Maharlika Investment Fund, evoking programmes and ideas from the dictatorship. His chapter ties in with others that do deep dives into subjects like agriculture and infrastructure. There’s a chapter on development challenges in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) written by Acram Latiph, a good reference on the region as it goes into a long-awaited election this September. Weena Gera, meanwhile, writes an illuminating chapter on the Mandanas-Garcia ruling of the Supreme Court that expanded the base for local governments’ share of revenues to include all national taxes. She argues that decentralisation, including Marcos’s current inclinations, fails to follow the maxim “finance follows function” and risks further dysfunction in providing local services. Many of these chapters offer policy recommendations that are evidence-based and well reasoned.

I enjoyed the cluster of chapters around the notion of Philippine politics being oligarchic in nature. What better way to enjoy the national soap opera than tales of cutthroat sibling rivalry? Athena Charanne Presto’s chapter on Marcos and his sister, Senator Imee Marcos, lays out the differences in their temperaments, talents, and strategies. Not enough is written about the Marcoses in their father’s bailiwick of Ilocos Norte, and this is where her work is quite revelatory. For example, the absenteeism and party boy image of Marcos Jr as president was already evident in abundance when he was the provincial governor. Snide remarks about the son not having the political acumen of the father were already being made about Junior when he was in local politics. As their father …

author: Salma Abdelrahman
title: Open call for proposals and reporting practices on artificial intelligence
content:
Everything is about AI now. On a general discourse level, a prophecy is being shoved down our throats telling us it is the one thing that is going to fundamentally change life as we know it.

The prophecy comes at us wrapped in the language of utopia and a tech giant’s latest market offering. Today, the capabilities of the computational power behind AI models are unprecedented, so much so that it may very well rival the cognitive skills of the human mind. AI is going to solve the mysteries of disease and eradicate world poverty, we are told. Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, has declared the arrival of “singularity,” the concept of machine intelligence surpassing human intelligence, two times now and still counting. Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google’s DeepMind, is the more cautious one: he only promises we are “near” it.

Based on these claims, hundreds of billions of dollars of capital are being thrown into AI-related investments, roughly 1 percent of global GDP. That is not counting the overall compulsion of businesses from all over the world to switch to AI, mainly out of fear of missing out on something big.

The implications are profound. Fantasies of replacing human labor that have been the obsession of capitalism for the past two centuries are reaching new heights with AI’s support. Data centers are being erected everywhere, doubling the global demand for copper. Operating them requires massive amounts of energy, leaving a larger carbon footprint on an already strained planet. Cooling them requires massive amounts of water. A Bloomberg analysis concluded that “two-thirds of new data centers built or in development since 2022 are in places already gripped by high levels of water stress.”

All this for an industry that has not only failed to generate revenue so far but that doesn’t even have any idea how it could do so in the future.

Despite all this, very little critical engagement is given to AI — except maybe the environmental impact.

Egypt is no stranger to this. In 2024, Egypt saw US$278 million in data center investments. The figure is projected to grow to $694 million by 2030. Every day in the press, you notice startups from different sectors and fields promising they will be providing AI-oriented solutions. “How exactly?” you might ask. No one actually knows.

This is an open call to invite those who are interested in this sort of critical engagement, both in the global context and with a focus on Egypt. While we do not want to restrict proposals, we are looking for approaches that open new ways of thinking about AI’s impact on the fundamentals of our lives. That means the proposals could be on fundamental subjects — labor, governance, health, environmental impact or entertainment — as much as on ways of approach — people’s history with AI, the political economy of AI or AI in the Global South. At the core, we are interested in trying to demystify the prophetic discourse surrounding AI and to look at the politics and power behind the claims that help themselves to grandeur. What really is behind this catchall that contains so much yet so little and that has thrust itself into every aspect of our lives?

As much as we are looking for concrete proposals, we also invite those who are interested in developing a practice of reporting on AI in Egypt to reach out — let’s have a conversation on how this could look like and what Mada Masr can provide to help.

Please reach out by email to submissions@madamasr.com, with a subject line of “Down with AI.”

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: When  the house is on fire
content:
With fires literally raging across the world, we return to a 2020 essay by Giorgio Agamben.

Other languages: Italiano, Español, Français, Nederlands, Português, Russian, Deutsch, Greek, Magyar, Türkçe

“Nothing I’m doing makes any sense if the house is on fire.” Yet even when the house is on fire it is necessary to continue as before, to do everything with care and precision, perhaps even more so than before—even if no one notices. Perhaps life itself will disappear from the face of the earth, perhaps no memory whatsoever will remain of what has been done, for better or for worse. But you continue as before, it is too late to change, there is no time anymore.

“What’s happening around you / is no longer your business”. Like the geography of a country that you must leave behind forever. Yet how does it still affect you? Precisely now that it is no longer your business, now that everything seems over, everything and every place now appears in its truest guise, somehow they all touch you even more intimately—just as they are: splendor and poverty.

Philosophy, a dead language. “The language of poets is always a dead language…it is a strange thing to admit: a dead language that one uses to provide greater life to thought.” Perhaps not a dead language, but a dialect. That philosophy and poetry speak in a language that is less than language is the measure of their rank, of their special vitality. To weigh and judge the world by measuring it against a dialect, a dead language that nevertheless pours forth anew, in which not even a comma can be changed. Keep speaking this dialect, even now that the house is on fire.

Which house is on fire? The country where you live, or Europe, or the entire world? Perhaps the houses and cities already burned down in some enormous fire—who knows how long ago—that we pretended not to notice. Of most of them all that remains are pieces of walls, a fresco, a patch of roof, names, so many names, already gnawed upon by flames. Nevertheless we carefully cover it all over with whitewash and falsified words, so that it looks intact. We live in houses and cities incinerated from one end to another as if they were still standing upright; people pretend to live in them and stroll in masks through ruins as if they were still in the familiar neighborhoods of a bygone era.

Today the flame has changed its form and nature, it has become digital, invisible and cold—but precisely for this very reason it is even closer still and surrounds us at every moment.

That a civilization—a barbarism—can sink, never to rise again, is nothing new. Historians are accustomed to identifying and dating caesuras and shipwrecks. But how can we bear witness to a world that is falling into ruin with eyes blindfolded and face covered, a republic collapsing with neither lucidity nor pride, but in abjection and fear? The blindness is all the more desperate since the shipwrecked claim to be governing their own shipwreck, they swear that everything can be controlled technically, that there is no need for either a new god or a new sky, only prohibitions, experts and doctors. Panic and villainy.

What would a God be to whom neither prayers nor sacrifices were addressed? And what would a law be that knew neither command nor enforcement? What is a word that has neither meaning nor command, but is truly held in the beginning—indeed, before the beginning?

A culture that feels it is at its end, that it has no life left, attempts to govern its decay in the only way it knows how, through a permanent state of exception. The total mobilization in which Jünger saw the essential character of our time should be understood from this perspective. People must be mobilized, they must feel themselves in a state of emergency at every moment, regulated down to the last detail by those who maintain the power to declare such an emergency. But whereas in the past mobilization sought to gather people together, today it aims to isolate them, to distance them from one another.

How long has the house been burning? How long since it burned down? Certainly a century ago, between 1914 and 1918, something happened in Europe that poured flames and madness upon everything that once seemed to remain intact and alive; then thirty years later, the flames again spread everywhere, and ever since have continued to burn without pause, submerged, barely visible beneath the cinders. But perhaps the fires began much earlier, when humanity’s blind impulse towards …

author: infolibre
title: Κάτω τα χέρια από το Κασμίρ! – Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης Παρασκευή 7/8 19:00 στη πλατεία Συντάγματος
content:
Κάτω τα χέρια από το Κασμίρ! Για να ακουστεί η φωνή του λαού του Κασμίρ!

ΓΙΑ ΝΑ ΑΚΟΥΣΤΕΙ Η ΦΩΝΗ ΤΟΥ ΛΑΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΚΑΣΜΙΡ!

Τους τελευταίους δύο μήνες το πακιστανικό κράτος έχει εξαπολύσει για μια ακόμα φορά δολοφονική καταστολή εις βάρος του πληθυσμού της αυτόνομης περιοχής του Αζάντ Κασμίρ, στο οποίο ασκεί τη διοίκηση. Το εθνικό κίνημα του Κασμίρ, υπό την ηγεσία του Κοινού Λαϊκού Συμβουλίου Δράσης (JAAC), πέτυχε τους τελευταίους μήνες δύο σημαντικές συμφωνίες με την κυβέρνηση του Αζάντ Κασμίρ, αλλά και την κεντρική πακιστανική κυβέρνηση. Οι συμφωνίες αυτές αφορούσαν αιτήματα για θεμελιώδη κοινωνικά και οικονομικά δικαιώματα, τα οποία όμως στην πράξη δεν ικανοποιήθηκαν στο ελάχιστο. Γι’αυτό από τις αρχές του Ιουνίου, ο λαός του Κασμίρ βρίσκεται σε κινητοποιήσεις στη Ραβαλακότ και άλλες μεγάλες πόλεις.

Η απάντηση του πακιστανικού κράτους ήταν η ανοιχτή καταστολή, με πραγματικά πυρά και δεκάδες (πάνω από 100) νεκρούς και τραυματίες. Η JAAC έχει κηρυχθεί εκτός νόμου ως τρομοκρατική οργάνωση και τα ηγετικά της στελέχη έχουν επικηρυχθεί ή συλληφθεί και απαχθεί, χωρίς κανείς να ξέρει πού βρίσκονται. Οι εκλογές που ήταν προγραμματισμένες να γίνουν στην περιοχή, γίνονται σταδιακά και υπό τέτοιες συνθήκες κρίσης και ανυποληψίας των θεσμών, που το ποσοστό συμμετοχής είναι ζήτημα αν ξεπερνάει το 7%. Ο λαός εξακολουθεί να βρίσκεται στους δρόμους, παρά το γεγονός ότι το πακιστανικό κράτος έχει κόψει κάθε οδική πρόσβαση, αλλά και το ηλεκτρικό ρεύμα και τις τηλεπικοινωνίες.

Απαιτούμε από το πακιστανικό κράτος να άρει την κατάσταση πολιορκίας, να εφαρμόσει τις συμφωνίες με το εθνικό κίνημα του Αζάντ Κασμίρ, και να σταματήσει τις διώξεις των ηγετών του, να επιτρέψει να γίνουν ελεύθερες και διαφανείς εκλογές, χωρίς τις στρεβλώσεις του εκλογικού νόμου που λειτουργούν ως μοχλός επιβολής κυβερνητικών στελεχών στην αυτόνομη κυβέρνηση. Ενώνουμε τη φωνή μας με τον καταπιεσμένο λαό του Κασμίρ, για να ακουστεί η φωνή του!

content:
By Arms Embargo Now, August 6, 2026

Less than a month after launching the #ElbitOutOfCanada campaign, we have already secured our first victory.

After receiving emails and a handwritten note from concerned community members, the Chief Operating Officer of Apollo Microwaves in Montréal reached out to inform us that they are no longer doing business with Elbit Systems and have no intention of resuming operations with the company in the future:

“There are no current orders for Elbit, and none will be accepted going forward,” the Chief Operating Officer wrote to the Arms Embargo Now Team.

And Apollo is not the only company we’ve heard from. It’s clear that our efforts to take an arms embargo into our own hands are working. Companies all across the country are paying attention— and some of them are already signalling a willingness to cut ties with Elbit to avoid public scrutiny.

But we’re just getting started. On August 13th, we’re putting local Elbit suppliers on notice from coast to coast to coast.

Together, we’re sending them a clear message: drop your ties with Elbit Systems or face the reputational and financial consequences of your ongoing complicity in Israel’s genocide.

Already, actions have been registered across the country and there’s still time to organize an action in your community! As the case of Apollo makes clear, sometimes all you need is a handful of people to put these companies on notice to compel them to cut their ties.

author: anred
title: Elles a la izquierda
content:
El movimiento feminista #NiUnaMenos concentra en el Congreso de la Nación – foto: Cristina Sille para Clarin

Un estudio difundido por la Fundación Faro, el think tank del oficialismo libertario, sostiene que existe una creciente brecha de género en la identificación política en Argentina. Los datos dialogan con investigaciones académicas realizadas en Europa, América Latina, Estados Unidos y Asia, que registran una tendencia similar: una mayor identificación de las mujeres con posiciones progresistas y un crecimiento de las preferencias conservadoras entre sectores de varones, especialmente jóvenes. Aunque el relevamiento de Fundación Faro es binario y se limita a las categorías de hombres y mujeres, distintos estudios coinciden en que estas transformaciones responden a procesos sociales, culturales y políticos mucho más amplios que una simple división por género. Por ANRed

Las investigaciones académicas desarrolladas en América Latina, Europa, Estados Unidos y Asia muestran que efectivamente existe una creciente brecha de género en la identificación política, especialmente entre las generaciones más jóvenes. Pero lejos de atribuirla a supuestas diferencias «naturales» entre mujeres y varones, los estudios la vinculan con procesos sociales y políticos: la expansión de los movimientos transfeministas, la reacción conservadora frente a la ampliación de derechos, las desigualdades económicas y el impacto de las redes sociales en la construcción de subjetividades políticas.

Fundación Faro. Publicación año 2025

En los últimos años, el ascenso de las nuevas derechas vino acompañado de una ofensiva contra los feminismos y los colectivos LGBTI+, convertidos en enemigos privilegiados de la llamada «batalla cultural». En ese escenario, la disputa por el sentido de la igualdad, los derechos sexuales y reproductivos, la educación sexual integral y las políticas de diversidad ocupa un lugar central en la construcción de identidades políticas.

Las investigaciones comparadas muestran que este fenómeno no es exclusivo de Argentina. Un estudio realizado en 36 países de la OCDE encontró que las mujeres comenzaron a ubicarse progresivamente más cerca de posiciones progresistas, mientras que entre muchos varones se observa un desplazamiento hacia posiciones conservadoras. Trabajos posteriores, realizados en Europa y América Latina, muestran que esa brecha se amplía sobre todo entre las juventudes, aunque con diferencias según el contexto político y cultural de cada país.

En América Latina, un análisis basado en las encuestas LAPOP detectó que entre las generaciones nacidas después de 1980 las mujeres expresan una mayor identificación con posiciones progresistas, mientras que los hombres muestran una mayor inclinación hacia opciones de derecha. Investigaciones realizadas en Corea del Sur, Estados Unidos y varios países europeos también registran un crecimiento de las posiciones antifeministas entre sectores de varones jóvenes, al mismo tiempo que muchas mujeres fortalecen su adhesión a agendas vinculadas con la igualdad de género y los derechos humanos.

Lejos de confirmar el relato de la Fundación Faro, estas investigaciones muestran que la brecha política no puede entenderse sin analizar las transformaciones del mundo del trabajo, la crisis de representación, el avance de los movimientos feministas y la reacción conservadora frente a la ampliación de derechos. Tampoco puede reducirse a una mirada binaria que deja fuera a las identidades travestis, trans y no binarias, actores fundamentales en las luchas contemporáneas por la igualdad.

Más que una «guerra entre hombres y mujeres», lo que expresan estos estudios es una disputa política e ideológica en torno al modelo de sociedad que se busca construir. Una disputa donde los feminismos, las organizaciones de la diversidad y los movimientos populares continúan enfrentando el avance de proyectos que buscan restringir derechos conquistados.

Diffondiamo il video e il comunicato uscito da La Base – Cosenza, Aula Studio Liberata e Fem.in Cosentine in Lotta

Non abbiamo mai avuto dubbi sulla dinamica che ha portato alla morte di Momo. Le parole della famiglia e di diversi abitanti del quartiere sono state chiare sin dall’inizio. Questo video, pubblicato da Iacchitè stamattina, fuga ogni altro dubbio. Mohamed è morto sotto la custodia dei carabinieri, gli stessi che hanno impedito alla madre di raggiungerlo al suolo. Momo era ammanettato e il carabiniere Restaneo gli ha tolto le manette mentre il corpo stramazzava.

Le responsabilità delle forze dell’ordine sono chiare e purtroppo la morte di Momo ci ricorda che questo non è un caso isolato, ma rappresenta la gestione sistemica del disagio sociale, che non cura, anzi, reprime. In particolare non è un caso che la maggior parte degli abusi avvengano su persone razzializzate e povere. Il governo, incapace di dare risposte sul piano dei servizi sociali e della garanzia dei diritti, si presenta con il suo volto più violento nelle nostre case e nelle nostre strade.

Il “sistema Cosenza” fatto dalla connivenza tra Procura, pezzi di borghesia e mala politica, impegnato affinché nulla cambi, ha già deciso come deve finire questa vicenda: insabbiare e silenziare come già è successo per altri casi. Le istituzioni hanno già preso posizione chiara: fare finta di nulla sperando che il tempo contribuisca a fare finire nel dimenticatoio il volto di Momo.

Noi non possiamo permettere tutto ciò, la richiesta di giustizia deve farsi incessante. Cosenza non accetterà mai l’ennesimo abuso di potere, lo ha dimostrato e lo dimostrerà.

author: Unknown
title: Chi sono i New IRA nel 2026 e di cosa sono ancora capaci?
content:
Il sequestro di una bomba contenente quasi 400 grammi di Semtex ha riacceso i riflettori sulla rete, sul reclutamento e sulla persistente minaccia rappresentata dal gruppo repubblicano dissidente.

Robin Schiller Irish Independent 31 luglio 2026

Il sequestro, avvenuto la scorsa settimana, di un ordigno contenente quasi 400 grammi di esplosivo plastico Semtex ha alimentato i timori che la New IRA sia riuscito ad accedere a nuove scorte di esplosivo di grado militare, in un momento di rinnovata attività violenta da parte dell’organizzazione repubblicana dissidente.

Sebbene le sue operazioni continuino a concentrarsi prevalentemente a nord del confine, la Garda ritiene che il «significativo» ordigno esplosivo recuperato mercoledì scorso nella contea di Monaghan sia stato assemblato a Dublino o nella sua area metropolitana, elemento che metterebbe in luce la dipendenza dell’organizzazione da una rete di attivisti operanti nella capitale.

Nonostante una consistenza stimata di appena un centinaio di membri, gli avvenimenti più recenti suggeriscono inoltre che il gruppo continui ad attrarre giovani appartenenti a una generazione nata molti anni dopo la fine dei Troubles, alimentando le preoccupazioni degli apparati di sicurezza circa la sua capacità di reclutare nuove leve e garantire continuità alla propria campagna armata.

Le indagini sul sequestro della scorsa settimana sono tuttora in corso e mirano ad accertare chi abbia costruito l’ordigno e a identificare gli altri soggetti coinvolti, nel tentativo di smantellare la rete del terrorismo repubblicano. L’episodio rappresenta l’ultimo grave incidente attribuito alla più recente incarnazione dell’Irish Republican Army.

Le origini

La New IRA nacque nel 2012 dalla fusione di militanti provenienti dalla Real IRA, da Republican Action Against Drugs (RAAD) e da numerosi altri piccoli gruppi repubblicani dissidenti contrari al processo di pace.

La sua costituzione segnò, di fatto, la fine della Real IRA, organizzazione attiva dal cessate il fuoco del 1997 e responsabile dell’autobomba di Omagh che, l’anno successivo, provocò la morte di ventinove persone. Nel 2012, inoltre, la Real IRA guidata da Alan Ryan aveva ormai perso gran parte della propria credibilità a causa dei suoi legami con attività criminali, comprese estorsioni ai danni di commercianti nella Repubblica d’Irlanda e il coinvolgimento in faide con gruppi della criminalità organizzata. Ryan fu ucciso nel settembre dello stesso anno su ordine di un importante esponente del crimine organizzato di Dublino.

Tra coloro ai quali venne affidato il compito di ricostruire la struttura dirigente del dissidentismo figuravano Kevin Braney, originario di Tallaght, destinato a diventare il responsabile della New IRA nell’area di Dublino, e Michael Barr, proveniente dalla contea di Tyrone. Padre di sei figli, Braney sarebbe stato successivamente nominato anche presidente di Saoradh per la città di Dublino, il movimento repubblicano radicale comunemente considerato dagli investigatori come il braccio politico della New IRA.

Poco dopo il suo trasferimento a Dublino, Barr venne arrestato insieme a Braney e ad altri cinque uomini nell’ambito di un’operazione condotta dalla Special Detective Unit (SDU) della Garda contro presunte attività dell’IRA.

Durante la perquisizione di un’abitazione a Tallaght, nel 2013, gli investigatori rinvennero comunicazioni provenienti da detenuti repubblicani rinchiusi nel carcere di Portlaoise, documenti che sarebbero stati fatti uscire clandestinamente dall’istituto penitenziario. Tutti gli arrestati furono incriminati con l’accusa di appartenenza all’IRA, ma il procedimento venne successivamente archiviato a causa di una questione procedurale.

Mentre la nuova organizzazione prendeva forma, episodi di violenza accompagnavano la sua nascita su entrambi i lati del confine.

Nel marzo 2013 il repubblicano dissidente Peter Butterly, trentacinquenne, venne assassinato all’esterno dell’Huntsman’s Inn di Gormanston, nella contea di Meath.

La Garda teneva sotto sorveglianza gli autori dell’omicidio già al momento dell’agguato e le informazioni raccolte permisero agli investigatori di registrarne segretamente le conversazioni nei giorni successivi, consentendo infine di ottenere sei condanne per l’assassinio.

author: Unknown
title: La repressione raccontata a mio figlio
content:
da Effimera, un articolo di Emanuele Braga

In un momento storico in cui un gruppo di fanatici bianchi e religiosi sta compiendo da quasi tre anni, in diretta streaming e protetto da uno degli eserciti più forti e tecnologicamente avanzati del mondo, il genocidio di un popolo oppresso. In un momento in cui, negli Stati Uniti, reparti speciali uccidono civili per strada attraverso vere e proprie esecuzioni sommarie e hanno il compito di deportare le persone non bianche presenti sul territorio nazionale. Gli stessi Stati Uniti che, pochi anni prima, hanno represso nel sangue — sotto governi di destra e di sinistra — le manifestazioni moltitudinarie esplose dopo il soffocamento, da parte della polizia, dell’ennesimo cittadino nero.

In Italia, nel luglio del 2026, Fakir è stato ucciso per soffocamento da due poliziotti durante un fermo. Era disarmato e chiedeva aiuto. Quella notte, a Bologna, migliaia di persone sono scese in piazza. Erano arrabbiate con la polizia. Strano.

In un’estate in cui Francia e Spagna bruciano, travolte da incendi alimentati dal caldo estremo, ventimila ecoattivistə si radunano sulle Alpi per il Festival Alta Felicità e assaltano ancora una volta il cantiere della TAV, dopo oltre vent’anni di lotte in difesa dell’ecologia e del territorio.

Come reagiscono i media davanti a tutto questo? Quasi tutti, compresi quelli più progressisti, sono impegnati a discutere del problema dei “violenti”, dai quali anche la sinistra parlamentare dovrebbe immediatamente prendere le distanze, pena la vittoria della destra.

Questa è la fotografia di quanto il dibattito pubblico, e gli esperti che hanno accesso al nostro sistema mediatico, siano oggi incapaci di rappresentare la realtà.

C’è molta gente arrabbiata perché i sistemi democratici e le istituzioni non riescono più a proteggerla, e quindi protesta. In fondo, la storia della politica si organizza intorno a questa tensione. Non intorno al modo in cui il campo largo dovrebbe posizionarsi a favore del tema della sicurezza per impedire l’ascesa di Vannacci.

La Storia, con la S maiuscola, si organizza intorno a due attori principali: i movimenti sociali e le forme attraverso cui si organizza il potere. E migliaia di anni di storia, più o meno, ci hanno mostrato questo: quando il modo in cui il potere viene amministrato esprime e tutela la collettività, il potere resta stabile; quando invece la opprime, la collettività reagisce, in forme più o meno conflittuali e violente.

La sinistra parlamentare ha quindi due possibilità: sgridare chi protesta, come fa Vannacci, oppure stare dalla parte di chi protesta, anche per impedire che Vannacci arrivi davvero al potere.

Il nostro giornalista di sinistra Michele Serra si sente invece in ostaggio di due fazioni: i manifestanti da una parte e i fascisti dall’altra. Vorrebbe poter vivere in un Paese di persone normali e ragionevoli come lui. Finisce così per equiparare ancora una volta gli oppressi ai loro seviziatori, evitando di vedere il punto politico essenziale: il mondo è già in fiamme.

Quando le suffragette incendiavano edifici e compivano azioni radicali per ottenere il diritto di voto, probabilmente la stampa laburista inglese di inizio Novecento fu impegnata a distinguere le donne “terroriste” da quelle che prendevano il tè discutendo educatamente di uguaglianza. Ma, anche se fosse stato così, oggi ci farebbe sorridere.

Perché la storia che abbiamo letto sui nostri sussidiari ci racconta altri attori: la vittoria finale della conquista del voto per le donne (sia quelle violente che quelle non) e un sistema industriale, capitalistico e patriarcale che aveva tutto l’interesse a mantenerle in una condizione di subordinazione e sfruttamento.

La verità è che abbiamo bisogno di intellettuali e giornalisti capaci di parlarci di questa Storia con la S maiuscola mentre leggono i fatti politici che accadono intorno a noi. Perché il dibattito pubblico che ci circonda è imbarazzante, moralista e del tutto inadeguato alla realtà che pretende di raccontare.

Cari giornalisti e classe dirigente nei media — Serra, Rampini, Mieli e tutti gli altri — che ora vi impegnate, da sinistra, a prendere le distanze dai cattivi maestri: fate un bel respiro e restate per un attimo in silenzio.

Cerco di spiegarvi il doppio standard che volete censurare come si spiegano le cose a chi finge di non capirle. C’è un mondo molto cattivo che, soffiando sul tema della sicurezza, cerca di imporre regimi sempre più repressivi. È composto da …

author: Unknown
title: La lotta di Bosco Ospizio
content:
Abbiamo raccolto alcune valutazioni sulla resistenza di questi giorni grazie a una chiacchierata svolta con un attivista di XR che partecipa alla lotta per la difesa di Bosco Ospizio a Reggio Emilia, buona lettura!

Lo chiamano Bosco Ospizio perché fino a 21 anni fa lì sorgeva un ospizio con un grande giardino alberato. Una volta demolito l’edificio principale, è iniziato un processo di rinaturalizzazione spontanea avviato grazie all’inaccessibilità all’area, perimetrata da una recinzione che impediva al pubblico di entrarvi.

Si è quindi originato un ambiente con le caratteristiche di un bosco urbano vero e proprio. Un ecosistema peculiare, 45 mila metri quadrati che hanno, oggi più che mai, effetti positivi inestimabili sul contesto urbano circostante, contribuendo a mitigare il calore urbano e ad assorbire gli inquinanti di un’area della città abitata soprattutto da anziani e fasce meno abbienti.

Circa undici anni fa l’area fu acquistata da Conad, soggetto particolarmente influente a Reggio Emilia, con l’obiettivo di realizzare un centro commerciale. Tra le opere di compensazione previste dall’intervento, Conad ha proposto la realizzazione di una Casa della Salute e di una biblioteca (quest’ultima già presente in passato ai tempi dell’ospizio e ora spostata non molto distante). Peccato però che tali opere corrispondano a meno di 2 mila metri quadrati di un progetto che prevede di cementificarne oltre 30 mila, che nelle carte del piano finanziario dell’Ausl Emilia-Romagna non risulti alcuna spesa per la Casa della Salute almeno fino al 2028 e che quest’ultima non compaia nemmeno nella programmazione delle future opere edilizie. Elementi che mettono in dubbio la reale volontà di realizzare il presidio sanitario annunciato.

Il progetto, a causa diversi ostacoli burocratici, non era comunque mai partito, ma un paio d’anni fa l’iter ha subito una forte accelerazione. Per contrastarla, viene formata l’Assemblea Bosco Ospizio, un comitato composto inizialmente da Ecologia Integrale, che ne rappresenta il riferimento tecnico, da Extinction Rebellion Reggio Emilia e Ripuliamoci Reggio Emilia, ai quali si è aggiunta successivamente Legambiente Reggio Emilia. Con il tempo si sono uniti numerosi cittadini e cittadine, dando vita a un’assemblea permanente e orizzontale che si riunisce ogni settimana e raccoglie persone di età e provenienza anche molto varie.

Le prime iniziative sono consistite in manifestazioni pubbliche e una raccolta firme per chiedere la convocazione di un Consiglio comunale aperto, uno strumento di partecipazione civica previsto nello statuto del Comune di Reggio Emilia, utilizzato per portare le istanze della cittadinanza all’amministrazione (per inciso, quello promosso dall’Assemblea Bosco Ospizio è stato il secondo Consiglio comunale aperto mai convocato nella città). Alla seduta del Consiglio l’aula viene riempita da sostenitori del comitato contrario al progetto mentre il fronte favorevole è invece rappresentato da una singola persona portavoce di un fantomatico comitato del Sì. In quella sede il comitato ha presentato studi, dati tecnici e analisi scientifiche sugli impatti sociali e ambientali che una simile colata di cemento avrebbe su un quartiere che, come scritto, è abitato prevalentemente da persone anziane e nuclei a basso reddito. L’obiettivo era fermare l’ultima firma necessaria al via libera definitivo, firma onere dell’Assessore alla rigenerazione urbana Pasini. L’amministrazione, tuttavia, ha sostenuto che gli accordi fossero ormai definitivi e di non avere più margini di intervento, respingendo pertanto le richieste del comitato (al che, ci chiediamo, perché quindi sarebbe stato necessario attendere questa firma?).

Durante lo stesso consiglio viene depositata una mozione popolare, a seguito di un’altra raccolta firme. La mozione verrà poi discussa in occasione di un altro consiglio comunale dedicato con data indicata dall’amministrazione. Tuttavia, due giorni prima, senza alcuna comunicazione pubblica, la stessa amministrazione aveva già apposto la firma sul progetto definitivo. Ancora una volta – i casi sono innumerevoli, gli schemi con cui si ripetono simili – all’esercizio di partecipazione concreta, alla capacità di onorare la democrazia e di costruire e applicare saperi tecnico-scientifici da parte della cittadinanza, certe amministrazioni rispondono in modo paternalista, sprezzante e truffaldino, sfiduciando strumenti che loro stesse hanno messo in campo, forse, non rimane che …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Sudan Nashra: Military builds on North Kordofan gains, prepares push into West Kordofan, repels RSF attempt to recapture West Darfur position along Chadian border | SPLM-N clashes with Otoro tribe inside Kauda | Third nationwide blackout in a week as financing impasse stalls electricity sector recovery | Stalled grid repairs put planting season at risk | Ethiopia fighting threatens Sudan’s largest rain-fed farming state
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here.

The military’s offensive in Kordofan continued this week with the capture of the strategic Jabal al-Dayer area near Rahad, building on last week’s gains that brought five towns and the Saderat Road linking Khartoum and Kordofan back under military control.

Military sources told Mada Masr the latest advance consolidates the military’s hold over southern and western North Kordofan while placing key routes into Rapid Support Forces-held areas in South Kordofan and West Kordofan under its control.

A senior military officer said that air strikes on remaining RSF positions in North Kordofan over the past week are also part of preparations for a simultaneous advance into the neighboring state.

Along the Chadian border, the RSF launched successive attacks on Bir Saliba and Hagar al-Marfaeen in West Darfur this week, but the military and allied forces repelled the assault after more than 12 hours of fighting. The area forms a key cross-border supply corridor linking the military’s positions in West Darfur with its operational bases in North Darfur.

In South Kordofan, a years-long dispute between the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North — the RSF’s ally led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu — and one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, has reached the movement’s seat of power.

Armed clashes broke out inside Kauda, its political and military headquarters, forcing residents to flee or shelter in their homes as markets, schools and public services shut down and transport into and out of the town came to a halt.

The confrontation is the latest stage in a dispute that began in 2022 over the SPLM-N’s moves to redraw administrative boundaries and reorganize tribal land ownership across the Nuba Mountains.

Since then, the disagreement has widened to include demands for greater political representation and participation in governing the movement’s territory, a member of the Otoro council of notables and a Kauda resident told Mada Masr.

Sudan’s grid collapsed for the third time in a week after a fault on a transmission line connected to the Merowe Dam triggered another nationwide outage.

Because damage from an RSF attack last year disabled voltage-control equipment at the dam and the war destroyed the grid’s central control facility, engineers said failures at individual stations can bring down the entire national network.

Those vulnerabilities were supposed to be addressed months ago, utility executives, engineers and officials in the energy and finance ministries told Mada Masr. But rehabilitation plans have remained frozen.

Merowe’s plan is not an exception. Across Sudan’s electricity sector, repair projects have piled up because public funds are absorbed by military operations and humanitarian response, and administrative reshuffles sometimes force procurement and approval procedures to start over.

Even if funding were released, the sector has steadily lost the engineers needed to carry out the work, driven out by the fighting and the rising cost of living, depriving the electricity system of what a former Energy Ministry official described as its “technical memory.”

Merowe’s electricity crisis is also putting the government’s wartime agricultural recovery plan at risk. Officials and engineers told Mada Masr that the plan to restore agricultural production in northern and eastern Sudan hinges on the same electricity infrastructure that has remained unrepaired, leaving farming dependent on electric-powered irrigation increasingly exposed to blackouts and load shedding during the peak growing season.

As the power crisis threatens irrigated farming, fighting that broke out in neighboring Ethiopia over the weekend is putting pressure on Gadarif, Sudan’s largest rain-fed farming state. Agricultural officials told Mada Masr that deteriorating insecurity along the border could disrupt planting, delay the movement of farming inputs and discourage financing at a critical stage of the growing season.

author: Ali Guidara
title: Anatomy of a Failure: How Tunisia’s Democracy Was Undermined
content:
Internal political betrayal, external cynicism, and the unravelling of the Arab Spring’s last laboratory.

On 25 July 2026, thousands of Tunisians took to the streets of central Tunis, not to mark the 69th anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic, but to denounce the power grab carried out exactly five years earlier by President Kais Saied. The demonstrators called for his resignation and an end to what they described as an increasingly authoritarian regime, accusing it of imprisoning dozens of political opponents, driving the country into economic decline, and dismantling the democratic experiment born of the 2011 revolution.

Yet the scenes stood in stark contrast to those of 25 July 2021. When Saied suspended parliament, dismissed the prime minister and concentrated power in his own hands, many Tunisians greeted his move not with alarm but with relief. A poll conducted by Emrhod Consulting at the time initially found an extraordinary 87 per cent approval rating for his actions. That largely forgotten figure serves as an uncomfortable reminder that the erosion of Tunisia’s post-revolution democratic experiment did not begin with the repression that followed, but with the popular embrace of a leader who promised to rescue a political system many had come to see as broken.

Saied did not destroy Tunisian democracy in a vacuum; he stepped into a house whose foundations had already been hollowed out from within.

Tunisia’s political crisis is not, at bottom, a crisis of personalities. It resurfaces decade after decade because its roots run deeper than any single ruler, reaching back more than sixty years to an institutional choice made at independence: the founders of the Republic placed the presidency, rather than a balance of powers, at the centre of the Tunisian state.

The 1959 Constitution borrowed heavily from France’s Fifth Republic, promulgated the year before. Like de Gaulle, Habib Bourguiba believed a strong executive was the surest bulwark against instability.

Each successive constitutional revision widened that gap. In 1975, Bourguiba was made president for life. Under his successor Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali, the same architecture hardened into full authoritarian rule — proof that Tunisian authoritarianism has never rested on any one man, but on a system built to accommodate him.

The First Betrayal Was Domestic

The 2011 revolution briefly broke the pattern: the 2014 Constitution divided power between president, government, and parliament for the first time since independence. But the experiment proved fragile — nine governments cycled through office in as many years, staffed by a political class with little experience of governing, its coalitions built to secure each party’s share of power rather than to solve the country’s problems. Ministries became spoils to defend, not instruments to deliver with, and the resulting improvisation left unemployment, regional inequality, and an unsustainable subsidy system unaddressed, government after government. Tunisians read that dysfunction as proof of a paralyzed state. But what exhausted them was the incompetence and self-interest of those who held power, not the parliamentary system itself — and conflating the two is exactly the trap that let the coup de force happen in 2021.

The Trap of a Temporary Measure

In July 2021, Saied invoked Article 80 of the 2014 Constitution to suspend parliament. What was promised as a temporary corrective has since hardened into a permanent system — and it has done so despite a spectacular collapse in public backing.

Saied’s 2022 constitution consecrated the return of a dominant presidency, sidelining parliament and government and restoring the vertical logic of 1959. Tellingly, the text put to referendum was not even the one drafted by the advisory commission Saied himself had appointed: its chair, the jurist Sadok Belaïd, publicly disowned the Saied’s version, warning that it paved the way to dictatorship.

The July 2022 constitutional referendum drew only 30.5 per cent of registered voters; the parliamentary elections that followed saw turnout of barely 11 per cent, among the lowest ever recorded.

By concentrating power in his own hands, Saied did not merely block political life: he also weakened the economy, the public services and narrowed the country’s room for manoeuvre in foreign policy.

It is at this critical juncture that the second betrayal took place: the geopolitical retreat of Tunisia’s Western partners …

author: Ismail Abukar
title: Somalia: The Journalists Who Disappeared
content:
In October 2022, Abdalle Ahmed Mumin — Secretary-General of the Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS), the organisation that documents what happens to journalists in Somalia — arrived at Aden Adde International Airport in Mogadishu carrying a ticket to Nairobi. He was travelling to seek medical care for injuries he had sustained during a previous detention.

He did not make his flight. According to documentation by the SJS and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), NISA officers detained him at the departure gate without a warrant, without stated charges, and without notifying his family or his organisation of where he was being taken. His apparent offence: he had issued a press statement ten days earlier expressing concern that a new government media directive was worded so broadly it would suppress legitimate journalism — and he had refused to retract it.

This was his first arrest. He was released, then arrested again when he attempted to travel for medical care. In February 2023, according to the SJS and RFK Human Rights, NISA officers detained him a third time. In his own public statements, as documented by the CPJ, he has said officers told him they would kill him if he resisted. According to the SJS and his own public account, he was held for thirty-three days and subjected to treatment that he has publicly described as torture. He was eventually released. Days later, as recounted by the SJS and IPI, a court order froze the SJS bank accounts, but no NISA officer involved in any of the three detentions was investigated, disciplined, or prosecuted.

Abdalle Ahmed Mumin returned to his desk.

“If I stop, they have won. If enough of us stop, there is no press left.”

— Abdalle Ahmed Mumin, Secretary-General, Somali Journalists Syndicate

That return — that refusal to stop — captures something about Somalia’s press freedom crisis that the international community is not fully seeing. The dominant narrative focuses on the journalists killed: seventy-three since the civil war began, according to the CPJ, with not one killing producing a conviction, according to CPJ records. That story is real and must be told. But alongside it, and increasingly supplanting it, runs a different and in some ways more calculated story: Somalia’s security apparatus has learned that arresting journalists is cheap, quiet, and equally effective.

Between 2007 and 2013, Al-Shabaab’s campaign against Somalia’s press was built on murder. Eighteen journalists were killed in 2012 alone — the highest single-year figure recorded in any country since. The killings generated international condemnation, press freedom resources, and diplomatic pressure. They were visible. Visibility, as those responsible eventually discovered, has costs.

The arrest figures tell the rest of the story. The SJS documented six journalist arrests by state security forces in 2015. By 2019, that figure had reached thirty-eight — a record, with thirty-seven journalists also beaten or threatened at gunpoint that year, predominantly by state forces rather than Al-Shabaab, according to the SJS. Between March and May 2025, the SJS and CPJ documented forty-one journalists arrested, assaulted, or harassed in sixty days. The International Press Institute (IPI) documented at least eighteen press freedom violations in Somalia in the second half of 2025 — among the highest totals recorded on the continent that period.

An overnight detention rarely makes international news. Confiscating footage, forcing a retraction, or freezing an organisation’s bank accounts achieves the same silencing effect as a death threat — at a fraction of the diplomatic cost. The journalist is silenced. The world does not notice. The officer who conducted the arrest faces no consequence.

Working as a human rights practitioner based in Mogadishu, I have observed alongside how detention is used as press suppression in Somalia, as has also been documented extensively by the SJS, the CPJ, and the US State Department. The patterns are consistent: arrest after publication to punish specific reporting; detention as leverage to force retraction; prolonged incommunicado holds designed to extract sources; newsroom raids to seize footage; and, most devastatingly, the targeting of the organizations that support journalists rather than only the journalists themselves.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Amid Growing Fears of Rogue AI, Expert Urges Governments to "Bring This to a Grinding Halt"
content: Is AI superintelligence inevitable? AI safety researcher David Krueger says it doesn’t have to be. Krueger, an assistant professor at the University of Montreal and founder of the nonprofit Evitable, warns that “we need to mitigate the risk of extinction” with regulation and moratoriums to halt the development of AI’s computational power and complexity, which he says is progressing at a rate much faster than current levels of human supervision can manage. Public statements from AI companies that their models have circumvented test constraints and broken into other systems are “what we should expect to happen with the way that we’re building AI, with how little we understand it and how primitive our techniques are for controlling it,” Krueger says. “We just don’t know how to build it safely. End of story.”

author: Roaa Reda
title: The dilemma of the ‘undeserving’: Families cut off from food subsidies describe prohibitively complex appeal process
content:
Walaa Mahdi, a resident of a Cairo neighborhood, is among the hundreds of thousands of people across the country who have found their government ration cards suddenly suspended this summer.

The smart card normally gives her and her family access to a basket of household essentials at state-subsidized prices: they get sugar, rice and oil via the card, as well as a daily quota of subsidized loaves.

When her card was suspended, she went to the local supply office to check its status. There, she discovered that her card was suspended on the grounds that her youngest son is enrolled in a private high school.

Mahdi was shocked by the suspension. The school is not a luxury for her son, but a hard-won investment their family is making in his education. They will pay the annual fee in installments, and her son is working alongside his studies to pay for the education. “How can this mean I am ‘underserving’ of support?” she wonders, speaking to Mada Masr.

Mahdi is not alone. She is one of at least 850,000 people the state has expelled from the subsidy program since June in a campaign it is pitching as “purifying operations” to rid the subsidy database of “undeserving” beneficiaries to improve the targeting of government resources.

Amid an outcry over the mass expulsions from citizens and their representatives in parliament, the Supply and Internal Trade Ministry has announced that families can appeal their cards’ suspension. The minister himself appeared on television last week to say that the appeals could be submitted at post offices, local supply offices and via the Digital Egypt platform for grievances, boasting the accuracy of the ministry’s ‘purification’ process by noting that only 2,600 appeals had been submitted so far.

But many of the families, as well as people working to support families’ appeal submissions, tell Mada Masr that even though they believe the expulsions have taken place in error, they have been unable to submit an appeal. They described the process as arduous, complex and bureaucratic.

As they and other families are suddenly pushed outside the support system, their exclusion has sparked concern that the government’s drive to purge “the undeserving” from the database will push households on the brink of coping further into economic difficulty and out of the scope of state protection.

Mahdi’s complaint is similar to that of Selim*, another Cairo resident who spoke to Mada Masr.

In his case, before the recent campaign, not all of his family were registered on the ration card, and for those who were registered, only some were entitled to receive general food subsidies, while others were only entitled only to receive a daily ration of subsidized bread.

Selim said that his card was suspended in recent weeks on the grounds that one of his sons was enrolled in a private school.

But while the government’s list of criteria says that families will be expelled if they pay school fees over LE20,000 per year, the fees for the private school his family member is enrolled in are no more than LE9,800 per year.

Enrolment of one or more children at a private or international school was among one of several criteria for suspending ration cards that the prime minister confirmed during a press conference in July. Other criteria include owning a “modern” car, residing at an upscale residential compound, owning a registered company and having a registered electricity consumption offense or receiving a government pension.

Ahmed, another resident speaking to Mada Masr, described finding his ration card suspended under the car ownership criteria, even though they sold their car years ago. Many on social media describe finding they have been disqualified for registered electricity offenses, even though they have been acquitted of those charges.

Mada Masr spoke with two people who have come across dozens of these cases. They work to provide digital and administrative services to residents in their local area for a fee, such as supporting families to file grievances, complete digital services like updating data or issuing birth certificates.

One of these service-providers in Sohag, Zain al-Abideen, explained that a majority of the people who have approached him about their ration card suspensions in recent weeks have been disqualified because of the private school enrollment criterion.

He also confirmed that while there are many complainants, only a few of them have got as far as submitting the formal appeal …

author: Abebe Woldeselassie
title: Why Ethiopia’s Conflicts Keep Returning: The Question Ethiopia’s National Dialogue Cannot Avoid
content:
As Ethiopia’s National Dialogue seeks to chart a path toward peace, it faces an immense task. The Dialogue aims to address some of the country’s most difficult political, historical, institutional, social, and peacebuilding questions. Yet its success may ultimately depend on confronting a more basic question: why do Ethiopia’s major conflicts keep returning?

Ethiopia’s National Dialogue Conference, Addis Ababa, 15 July 2026

A problem relocated, not resolved

One answer lies in a problem that has received too little attention. The challenge of nation-building was not resolved after 1991; it was relocated. As political authority came to be organised through ethnoregional states, regional governments became central arenas for managing recognition, representation, and self-government.

This is not an argument against recognition or self-government. Recognition and autonomy expanded opportunities for political participation, representation, and self-rule. But they also changed the way political competition worked. Regional governments became more than administrative units. Through language policy, education, administration, media, public narratives, and territorial claims, regional institutions have often created hierarchies of belonging rather than equal citizenship, making some citizens appear more native, legitimate, or entitled than others. Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts are therefore not only about power. They are also about a system that made identity, territory, representation, and authority increasingly hard to separate.

As these institutions matured, political competition increasingly centred on the representation and defence of communities defined by territory and identity. Contests over leadership, resources, or administration have become securitized struggles over status, belonging, and political survival. While institutions do not cause violence by themselves, they can encourage political actors to present territorial control as a matter of group survival. Losing political power is often experienced not simply as an electoral setback, but as a threat to a group’s place in the political order.

Wolkait, and what it really reveals

This becomes clearest where territory intersects with competing claims of belonging and authority. The Wolkait conflict illustrates the point. Although often presented as a conflict over administrative boundaries, it also reflects deeper questions about membership, government, and the political meaning of territory. Historical claims, constitutional arrangements, ethno-linguistic boundaries, land grievances, displacement, and Ethiopia’s post-1991 regional order all matter. But they do not fully explain why Wolkait became so politically consequential.

The conflict is also about political belonging: who is treated as native, who is seen as a recent settler, and whose authority is considered legitimate. For many Tigrayans, Wolkait’s incorporation into Tigray became part of regional self-government. For many Amharas, it symbolised exclusion from land they regard as historically theirs. It is therefore not only about maps or legal status. It is also about land, memory, identity, representation, and authority.

Wolkait is not an isolated case. Similar patterns appear elsewhere, even when the histories and grievances differ. Addis Ababa offers another example. Its layered history and diverse population show how difficult it is to fit lived belonging into a single ethnic-territorial frame. The continuing conflicts involving the Oromo Liberation Army, an armed Oromo insurgent group, and Fano, a loosely organised Amhara militia movement, illustrate how struggles over security, recognition, and authority become tied to claims about belonging.

Persistent insecurity, displacement crises, and identity-targeted violence across Ethiopia point to a deeper problem. When authority is tied closely to identity and land, basic questions of residence and administration become politically explosive. Politics becomes less about policy or public services, and more about membership, recognition, and control over political space. The human-rights costs can be severe for many citizens, but they are especially acute for people seen as outsiders in the places they live.

This deeper tension is not new. For much of the post-1991 period, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front, or EPRDF, contained it through elite bargaining, central control, and a powerful security apparatus. But containment was …

title: Captivus - En fattig mans visa
content:
Författare

: Captivus

Titel

: En fattig mans visa

Källa

: Tidningen Brand #8 1915


 Väl går jag i husen och tigger min mat,

 får snäsor av pigor och skälles för lat

 och hotas ibland med polisen.

 Men jag är en karl, som är lycklig ändå,

 om blott jag kan få

 mig värma en stund invid spisen.


 Därute är kallt och disande grått,

 men glöden i spisen mig värma så gott,

 när pannorna steka och fräsa.

 Jag drömmer mig himlen ett jättestort kök

 i kok och i stök,

 när matlukten kittlar min näsa.


 Och när jag har värmt mig och ätit mig mätt,

 jag tackar förnöjd på mitt noblaste sätt

 min kindröda kökshärskarinna.

 Det lider mot kväller, jag säger god natt,

 men vore jag katt

 nog låge jag kvar för att spinna.

 När telegrafen knackade din död

 på några vita smala pappersramsor,

 all världen lyssnade, när salvan ljöd

 som söndersköt ditt starka bröst i slamsor.


 Men redan lagra dagarna sitt dam

 Men utav unga sitter än en ring

author: David Swanson
title: Nonviolent Citizen Resistance Moves the World Social Forum Forward in Benin
content:
By Guy Feugap, Africa Organizer, World BEYOND War, August 5, 2026

After a long period of uncertainty that raised fears of the cancellation of the 2026 World Social Forum, the Government of Benin finally authorized this important gathering of social movements to take place. World BEYOND War welcomes this decision and the power of nonviolent action by civil society.

The African Organizer of World BEYOND War arrived in Cotonou on August 3, 2026, to contribute to the Forum through several initiatives, including the official launch of the World BEYOND War Benin chapter and a series of international dialogues on war in Sudan. The Forum’s opening march, along with other activities planned at the official venue, could not take place because of a last-minute cancellation by the Government of Benin. These events are regrettable at a time when Africa is facing armed conflicts, humanitarian crises, and growing militarization. Spaces for dialogue, cooperation, and peacebuilding such as the World Social Forum are more necessary than ever. It is paradoxical that a continent suffering so deeply from the consequences of war should trivialize a gathering dedicated to peace and international solidarity.

Faced with this situation, the participating organizations did not give into discouragement. They multiplied consultations, coordinated their positions, and continued their exchanges in a spirit of solidarity and nonviolence. This calm and determined mobilization helped maintain pressure in favor of holding the Forum and reminded everyone of the importance of respecting civic freedoms and spaces for dialogue.

The decision of the Beninese authorities to finally authorize the Forum is an encouraging signal. It shows that peaceful citizen mobilization can produce concrete results. This development represents a victory for the organizations present in Cotonou, and also for all those who believe in the power of nonviolent action to defend rights, democracy, and peace.

World BEYOND War congratulates all the social movements, the organizations present in Cotonou, and the thousands of activists who remained mobilized throughout this period of uncertainty. We also welcome the arrival of the West African Peace Caravan, now authorized to join the Forum. We express our solidarity with the participants who were deported at Benin’s borders. The challenges facing Africa and the world require more dialogue, more cooperation, and more solidarity. World BEYOND War will participate in the Forum with even greater commitment and will work with African and international movements to build a world beyond war, founded on justice, common security, and human dignity.

La résistance citoyenne non violente fait avancer le Forum social mondial au Bénin Guy Feugap, Organisateur Africain de World BEYOND War

author: Greta Zarro
title: Volunteer Spotlight: Baltimore Chapter Co-Coordinator Ronda Cooperstein
content:
Each month, we share the stories of World BEYOND War volunteers around the world. Want to volunteer with World BEYOND War? Email greta@worldbeyondwar.org.

I became an anti-war activist at a young age, after reading many books about Indigenous peoples across the globe. I was shocked and appalled at the violence inflicted on so many innocent populations in the name of civilization. Once in college, in the late 70’s, I became active on campus, joining and supporting groups that worked for peace and justice. As a Jewish American, I became very active in issues related to Israel/Palestine and went on to found a local organization, Baltimore Jews for Israeli Palestinian Peace. After years and years of working locally on these issues, I decided to start a chapter of World BEYOND War in Baltimore. I was inspired by the Ukrainian conscientious objector, Yurii Sheliazhenko, who is a Board Member of World BEYOND War.

Our local chapter, since forming a little over a year ago, has worked mainly on issues related to Israel/Palestine, hosting Combatants for Peace, bringing Israeli genocide scholar Omer Bartov to Baltimore, and holding vigils. We also lobby our Congress members to support all anti-war legislation and to take a stand against militarism at all levels. Last summer we co-sponsored the local Hiroshima/Nagasaki Memorial event. In the fall, we will be bringing WBW Co-Founder and Executive Director David Swanson to Baltimore.

My top recommendation for someone who wants to get involved is to remember that no act on behalf of peace is too small, that every person counts, that kindness and solidarity at all levels are the keys to moving forward.

What keeps me inspired is knowing that we are responsible for one another, for the Earth and all its inhabitants, human and non-human. Therefore, the extraordinary violence and cruelty of the U.S. government and its allies can never be ignored.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”: Jornada Federal contra la extranjerización de la tierra
content:
Este jueves 6 de agosto, mientras el Senado se disponga a debatir la denominada “Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada”, un amplio marco de organizaciones campesinas, indígenas, ambientales, sociales, políticas, de derechos humanos y sindicales realizarán una jornada federal de protesta en distintos puntos del país. La convocatoria central será frente al Congreso Nacional, bajo la consigna “La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”, en rechazo a un proyecto que denuncian como un nuevo avance sobre los territorios y los bienes comunes. La jornada incluirá una radio abierta, un “verdurazo” y un festival cultural. También habrá acciones en otros puntos del mundo, como Berlín (Alemania). Las organizaciones sostienen que la iniciativa legislativa se inscribe en una política de profundización del extractivismo y de apertura al capital extranjero que, junto al RIGI y otras reformas impulsadas por el gobierno de Javier Milei, amenaza con acelerar los desalojos, la concentración de la tierra y la pérdida de soberanía territorial.

Mientras el Senado se prepara para debatir este jueves 6 de agosto la denominada Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada, organizaciones indígenas, campesinas, ambientales, sociales, políticas, sindicales y de derechos humanos convocan a una jornada federal de movilización para rechazar una iniciativa que consideran un nuevo avance sobre los territorios, los bienes comunes y la soberanía nacional.

Las actividades comenzarán hoy, miércoles 5 de agosto a las 12, con un “Culturazo en defensa de la tierra y la soberanía” y una conferencia de prensa en el Teatro Picadero (Pasaje Enrique Santos Discépolo 1857, CABA), impulsada de forma conjunta por la Coordinadora Plurinacional Basta de Falsas Soluciones (BFS), Actrices Argentinas, el Colectivo de Acción por la Justicia Ecosocial (CAJE) y la Asociación Argentina de Abogados/as Ambientalistas. Allí, las organizaciones presentarán públicamente los fundamentos de su rechazo al proyecto, sosteniendo que la ley forma parte de un paquete de reformas que favorecen la concentración de la tierra, profundizan los desalojos y fortalecen un modelo basado en el extractivismo y la mercantilización de los bienes comunes.

En tanto, bajo la consigna “La tierra no se vende, no se quema, ni se desaloja”, este jueves 6 de agosto la convocatoria central será desde el mediodía frente al Congreso Nacional, donde habrá radio abierta, un festival cultural, un “verdurazo” y distintas intervenciones durante toda la jornada.

También, desde las 18 tendrá lugar frente al Congreso Nacional el “Festival en Lucha”, con la participación Willy Bronca y Malena D’Alessio, que contará también con la lectura de un documento conjunto a cargo de Charo López, Juan Solá, Maite Lanata, Jazmín Stuart y Adolfo Pérez Esquivel.

Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por Coordinadora Plurinacional BFS (@bastadefalsassoluciones)

De la movilización al Congreso Nacional también participarán desde la Confederación de Combatientes de Malvinas por considerar que “el proyecto impulsado por el gobierno nacional se trata de una claudicación de soberanía sin precedentes” y que “este gobierno maltrata a su pueblo, agobia a sus jubilados, quita educación y salud, y no cuestiona que magnates como Benetton, Lewis y otros grandes grupos económicos continúen expropiándose vastas extensiones de la Argentina”. En ese sentido, remarcan: “la doble vara es evidente: se ataca lo publico y se protege la concentracion y extranjerizacion de la tierra”.

Quienes ofrecieron su vida y su integridad física en defensa de nuestras Islas Malvinas en 1982 acaban de lanzar un comunicado afirmando que van a marchar este 6 de agosto en contra de la ley y en defensa de nuestro territorio y los recursos naturales pic.twitter.com/RKL61bafaG — Rattenbach (@jmrosas1845) August 4, 2026

Las movilizaciones y acciones tendrán alcance nacional. Además de la protesta frente al Congreso Nacional mientras el Senado esté tratando el proyecto, habrá actividades en varias localidades del país, como Baradero, Mar del Plata, Rosario, Córdoba, Mendoza, Tucumán, La Pampa, Jujuy, Salta, Bariloche (Río Negro), Comarca Andina (Chubut), Posadas (Misiones), Paraná (Entre Ríos) y Ushuaia, Río Grande y Tolhuin (Tierra del Fuego), según relevó la cuenta de instagram de Rebelión o Extinción .
